items.item: 1. 'The Thirsty Crow' (तृष्णार्तः काकः): where the story comes from
items.verdict: CONFIRMED as an Aesopic fable. I found no classical Indian version (Pañcatantra, Hitopadeśa or Jātaka). Websites and children's books that call it 'a Pañcatantra story' are using a modern label that no Sanskrit text supports. It is common in Indian school readers today: confirmed for a Sanskrit reader and for Hindi retellings, not confirmed for NCERT.
items.evidence: (a) Wikipedia, 'The Crow and the Pitcher' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crow_and_the_Pitcher): no. 390 in the Perry Index. Treated in a poem by Bianor (1st c. CE), in pseudo-Dositheus (2nd c.) and in Avianus's Latin verse fables (4th–5th c.; Latin title 'De cornice et urna'). Avianus's moral is that cleverness beats brute strength. The fable's history is traced in A.E. Wright, 'Hie lert uns der meister'. (b) Pliny, Natural History Book 10 (Rackham Loeb §125; Bostock–Riley ch. 60) tells of a thirsty bird heaping stones into a rain-filled urn on a monument. Translations differ between crow and raven, and Pliny says only that 'certain persons have thought it worth recording' (Perseus, LacusCurtius/Holland, Loeb LCL 353). (c) Searches for a Pañcatantra, Hitopadeśa or Jātaka version found no Sanskrit or Pāli text. They found only modern retellings branded 'Panchatantra': Penguin India 2003 'The Crow and the Pitcher: Based on a tale from the Panchatantra' (a loose blend with a modern subplot), a Tribune column and podcasts. (d) Present-day use: the UP Board Class 5 Sanskrit reader 'संस्कृत पीयूषम्' has the lesson 'काकस्य उद्यमः' (chapter 10 or 16 depending on edition; its vocabulary includes पिपासा and पाषाण-खण्डानि) (studiestoday.com, selfstudys.com). Hindi 'प्यासा कौआ' retellings are everywhere, and the fable appears in Bangladeshi English exam materials. I could not confirm that NCERT includes it, so the course should not name NCERT.
items.course_wording: HISTORY callout: "This story does not come from ancient India. It is a fable of the Greek and Latin Aesopic tradition, 'The Crow and the Pitcher' (no. 390 in B.E. Perry's catalogue of Aesop's fables). It first appears in a Greek poem by Bianor (1st century CE) and in the Latin fables of Avianus (around 400 CE), whose moral is that cleverness beats brute strength. Pliny the Elder reports the same trick as something a real crow was seen doing. No version is known from the Pañcatantra, the Hitopadeśa or the Jātakas. Today it is one of the best-known children's stories in India (Hindi प्यासा कौआ) and appears in Sanskrit school readers. Our Sanskrit telling is new, written for this course." Teacher Note: "Some books call it 'a Pañcatantra story'. That label is modern, and no Sanskrit text of the Pañcatantra contains this fable."
items.ref: no key. Needs new REFERENCES entries: (1) perry1952: B.E. Perry, *Aesopica: A Series of Texts Relating to Aesop or Ascribed to Him or Closely Connected with the Literary Tradition That Bears His Name*, vol. 1: Greek and Latin Texts, Urbana: University of Illinois Press, 1952 (the Perry Index; no. 390). (2) duff1934: J.W. Duff & A.M. Duff (eds./trs.), *Minor Latin Poets*, Loeb Classical Library 284, Cambridge MA: Harvard University Press, 1934 (Avianus, Fabulae, 'De cornice et urna'; fable number not verified in this session). (3) rackham1940: Pliny the Elder, *Natural History* vol. III (Books 8–11), tr. H. Rackham, Loeb Classical Library 353, Harvard University Press, 1940, Book 10 §125.
items.register: HISTORY for the origin and attestation. FACT with a present-day usage label for its use in Indian school readers.

items.item: 1b. A related claim you are likely to meet: a Harappan jar from Lothal shows the thirsty crow
items.verdict: UNVERIFIED and speculative. Do not use it.
items.evidence: A popular article (differenttruths.com), a 2025 IJFMR paper that says only 'probably depicts', and a reader's note on Tony Joseph's 'Early Indians' (Goodreads) read a miniature Lothal jar with a crow, a pitcher and a deer as the thirsty-crow scene. None of them cites an excavation report. The better-known Lothal identification is a jar with birds holding fish and a fox-like animal below (Indian Culture Portal; S.R. Rao, Lothal 1985, as cited on a blog). That one is linked to the 'cunning fox' story, not to the crow and the pitcher, and it is itself an interpretation.
items.course_wording: Leave it out of lessons. If a teacher asks: "Some popular writers read a painted jar from Lothal as this story, but archaeologists have not established that reading, so the course does not teach it." Suggest adding it to the 1.x-style 'documented errors' list if it ever appears in drafts.
items.register: Excluded. At most a hedged line in Teacher Notes.

items.item: 2. 'The Lion and the Mouse' (सिंहः मूषकः च): where the story comes from
items.verdict: CONFIRMED as an Aesopic fable (Perry 150), with an ancient Egyptian parallel. No lion-and-mouse story as such was found in the Pañcatantra or Hitopadeśa. The closest classical Indian parallels are the Pañcatantra story of mice freeing elephants (see item 3) and the mouse who gnaws through a net (see item 4).
items.evidence: (a) Wikipedia, 'The Lion and the Mouse' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lion_and_the_Mouse): Perry Index no. 150. In the earliest versions a mouse wakes the lion and is spared; later the lion is netted by hunters and the mouse gnaws through the ropes. The usual moral is that mercy is rewarded and no creature is too small to help a greater one. (b) attalus.org 'Solar eye' (https://attalus.org/egypt/solar_eye.html), adapted from M. Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature III (1980), pp. 157–159: the Demotic 'Myth of the Sun's Eye' (Leiden Demotic Papyrus I 384, 2nd c. CE) contains a fable in which a lion spares a mouse, and when the lion is caught in a trap the mouse bites through the rope and frees him. A Greek translation survives in fragments. (c) The Babrius number (107) could not be verified, so leave it out. (d) Some claims are unsupported and must not be used: that Aesop copied the Hitopadeśa (a Vanisource lecture page), and that the lion-and-mouse tale itself is 'in the Panchatantra' (storymuseum.org.uk). Perry's own hypothesis about Greek influence on some Indian fables is described as controversial, so the course should make no claim about which way stories travelled. (e) Present-day use: the UP Board Class 3 Sanskrit lesson 'लघुः अपि सहायकः' retells this story, and its vocabulary lists कृन्तामि.
items.course_wording: HISTORY callout: "This too is an Aesopic fable, 'The Lion and the Mouse' (no. 150 in Perry's catalogue). The same tale, in which a lion spares a mouse and the mouse later gnaws through the ropes that hold the lion, is also told inside an Egyptian story written down in Demotic in the 2nd century CE. India's own fable books have a cousin of it: in one version of the Pañcatantra, mice repay a herd of elephants by gnawing them free from hunters' nets. Fables like these travelled widely. Scholars do not agree on how, and the course makes no claim about which came first. Our Sanskrit retelling is new."
items.ref: [REF:panchatantra Book 2 (Pūrṇabhadra recension), the mice and the elephants]. Also no key. Needs new entries: perry1952 (as in item 1; no. 150). lichtheim1980: M. Lichtheim, *Ancient Egyptian Literature: A Book of Readings*, vol. III: The Late Period, Berkeley: University of California Press, 1980, pp. 157–159 (lion-and-mouse fable in the Myth of the Sun's Eye, Leiden Demotic Papyrus I 384; page range from attalus.org, check against the book). ryder1925 (see item 3).

items.item: 3. The Pañcatantra story of mice freeing elephants: exact locus
items.verdict: PARTLY VERIFIED. Confirmed in Pūrṇabhadra's recension (1199 CE), Book 2 ('The Winning of Friends', Mitrasaṃprāpti/Mitralābha). It is told by the deer Citrāṅga ('Spot' in Ryder) during the episode of his capture in a snare. Ryder's title is 'The Mice That Set Elephants Free', and the story closes with the verse 'Make friends, make friends, however strong or weak they be: / Recall the captive elephants that mice set free.' Not verified: whether the story is in the textus simplicior (the default text of the `panchatantra` key), in Edgerton's reconstruction or in Olivelle's translation; any story or verse number; the Sanskrit wording of the closing verse.
items.evidence: Wikisource, 'The Panchatantra (Purnabhadra's Recension of 1199 CE)/Book 2/The Mice That Set Elephants Free' (Ryder 1925 translation) (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Panchatantra_(Purnabhadra's_Recension_of_1199_CE)/Book_2/The_Mice_That_Set_Elephants_Free). Ryder's table of contents and the LibriVox recording place it in Book II, between 'Hang-Ball and Greedy' and 'Spot's Captivity'. Wikipedia's 'List of Panchatantra stories' says Pūrṇabhadra's recension underlies Ryder 1925 and Rajan 1993; a garbled snippet of its table may place the tale differently in another version, which I could not read. Sanskrit searches (sa.wikisource, vishvasa.github.io, wisdomlib Book 2) did not surface the episode. Hindi 'गजराज और मूषकराज' versions are modern retellings with added details and are not evidence for the Sanskrit text.
items.course_wording: "In Pūrṇabhadra's version of the Pañcatantra (1199 CE), in Book 2, 'Winning Friends', the deer Citrāṅga tells how mice once freed a herd of elephants caught in hunters' nets." Always name the recension. Give no story or verse number, and do not write 'the Pañcatantra says' without qualification.
items.ref: [REF:panchatantra Book 2, Pūrṇabhadra recension, 'The Mice That Set Elephants Free'] (the key says 'textus simplicior unless noted', so the recension must be stated). No key for the translation. Needs new entry ryder1925: Arthur W. Ryder (tr.), *The Panchatantra*, Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1925 (translated from Pūrṇabhadra's recension of 1199 CE), Book II, 'The Mice That Set Elephants Free'.
items.register: HISTORY for the textual locus. TRADITION if the story itself is retold, attributed to the named recension.

items.item: 4. Another Indian parallel: a mouse gnaws through a net (Pañcatantra Book 2 frame story; Hitopadeśa Book 1, Mitralābha)
items.verdict: CONFIRMED
items.evidence: vishvasa.github.io, Pañcatantra 2 Mitrasaṃprāpti, 'लघुपतनक-चित्रग्रीव-कथा': the mouse Hiraṇyaka cuts the snare holding the pigeon king Citragrīva and his flock. Hitopadeśa, Arnold's translation (franpritchett.com, 1_winningfriends): 'Golden-skin … began to gnaw the strings that held Speckle-neck'. A SOAS illustrated-manuscript record describes the same episode.
items.course_wording: Optional enrichment for §4 or §17: "In the opening story of Pañcatantra Book 2, and of the first book of the Hitopadeśa, the mouse Hiraṇyaka gnaws through a fowler's net to free the pigeon king Citragrīva and his flock."
items.ref: [REF:panchatantra Book 2, frame story]; [REF:hitopadesha mitralābha, frame story]
items.register: TRADITION (story content attributed to named texts)

items.item: 5. Crow sentences 1–5: एकः काकः अस्ति। सः तृष्णार्तः अस्ति। सः जलम् इच्छति। सः एकम् घटम् पश्यति। घटे अल्पम् जलम् अस्ति।
items.verdict: CORRECT. One wording preference: पिपासितः is the clearer word for 'thirsty'.
items.evidence: एकः meaning 'a (certain)' is acceptable in a graded reader; classical narration would use कश्चित् and the past tense आसीत्, both outside the toolkit. तृष्णार्त is attested: Mahābhārata 14.31.8 has tṛṣṇārtaḥ, glossed 'afflicted by thirst/desire' (enjoylearningsanskrit.com). But तृष्णा also means 'craving', so the word is ambiguous. पिपासित 'thirsty, athirst' (MW, via kosha.sanskrit.today) is unambiguous, and the UP Board version builds on पिपासा. घट (m.) means 'jar, pitcher'. एकम् घटम् is accusative and घटे is locative, both taught as whole-word glosses. अल्पम् is the v2.c05 quantity word and agrees with जलम्. The pause-form spellings एकम् घटम् are fine; the sandhi forms would be एकं घटं.
items.course_wording: एकः काकः अस्ति। सः पिपासितः अस्ति। (or keep तृष्णार्तः, glossed 'thirst-stricken') सः जलम् इच्छति। सः एकम् घटम् पश्यति। घटे अल्पम् जलम् अस्ति। Optional problem line: जलम् अधः अस्ति। ('the water is down low').

items.verdict: GRAMMATICAL BUT BREAKS THE TOOLKIT. पाषाणान् is accusative PLURAL, and the toolkit is singular only. The sentence also says nowhere where the stone goes (no 'into the pot').
items.evidence: √क्षिप् 'throw' is tudādi (class 6): क्षिपति. पाषाण (m.) means 'stone' (MW). The UP Board reader uses the neuter plural पाषाण-खण्डानि. 'Throws stones', with no location, does not say that they go into the pot.
items.course_wording: सः एकम् पाषाणम् घटे क्षिपति। सः पुनः पुनः क्षिपति। ('He throws a stone into the pot. Again and again he throws.' पुनः is already in the ledger from v2.c05.) The 'one by one' idiom एकैकम् can come later.
items.ref: [REF:dhatupatha tudādi क्षिप्]; [REF:apte1890 s.v. क्षिप्]; [REF:monierwilliams1899 s.v. pāṣāṇa]

items.verdict: ACCEPTABLE
items.evidence: Here उपरि is an indeclinable adverb, 'above, up(wards)'. आगच्छति was taught in v2.c05.l01. The classical synonym ऊर्ध्वम् is also possible.
items.course_wording: जलम् उपरि आगच्छति। (gloss उपरि 'up'). Optional: शनैः शनैः जलम् उपरि आगच्छति। ('slowly the water comes up').

items.item: 8. सः जलम् पिबति। सः सुखी भवति।
items.verdict: CORRECT
items.evidence: सुखी is the nominative singular masculine of the in-stem सुखिन् 'happy'. Teach it as a whole word, because in-stems come later. An a-stem alternative is तृप्तः 'satisfied, with thirst quenched' (participle of √तृप्).
items.course_wording: सः जलम् पिबति। सः सुखी भवति। (or सः तृप्तः भवति।)

items.item: 9. The crow's moral: बुद्धिः बलात् श्रेष्ठा।
items.verdict: UNDERSTANDABLE AND COMMON IN MODERN SANSKRIT, BUT NOT THE TEXTBOOK CLASSICAL CONSTRUCTION. श्रेष्ठ is a superlative ('best'). In classical Sanskrit, 'than' + ablative goes with a comparative. The pattern 'X से श्रेष्ठ' is Hindi. Its meaning does match Avianus's moral (cleverness over strength).
items.evidence: Whitney §292b: the ablative is 'the regular and almost constant construction' after a comparative or a word used in a similar way. Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.42 पञ्चमी विभक्ते; the Kāśikā example is माथुराः पाटलिपुत्रकेभ्यः आढ्यतराः (comparative + ablative). For superlatives, 2.3.41 यतश्च निर्धारणम् prescribes the genitive or locative of the group (Kāśikā: मनुष्याणां/मनुष्येषु क्षत्रियः शूरतमः) (sanskritdocuments.org Aṣṭādhyāyī vyākhyā). Classical model: Bhagavadgītā 3.35 śreyān svadharmo viguṇaḥ paradharmāt svanuṣṭhitāt. I could not retrieve whether MW records śreṣṭha + ablative from the epics, so treat श्रेष्ठा + ablative as non-standard rather than impossible. A genuine classical saying on the same theme is in the Hitopadeśa (wisdomlib numbering 2.122): बुद्धिर्यस्य बलं तस्य निर्बुद्धेस्तु कुतो बलम्, followed by the lion-and-hare line. It is widely quoted as from the Pañcatantra too, but that locus was not verified.
items.course_wording: Preferred: बुद्धिः बलात् श्रेयसी। ('Intelligence is better than strength.' Gloss बलात् 'than strength' and श्रेयसी 'better (f.)' as whole words.) A version using only nominatives: बुद्धिः एव बलम्। ('Intelligence itself is strength'; written for the course, not a quotation.) Optional TRADITION callout: "The Hitopadeśa says: बुद्धिर्यस्य बलं तस्य — 'whoever has intelligence has strength.'"
items.ref: [REF:whitney1889 §292b]; [REF:ashtadhyayi 2.3.41–42]; [REF:kashika 2.3.42]; [REF:bhagavadgita 3.35]; for the optional quotation [REF:hitopadesha 2.122] (wisdomlib/Satya Narayana Dasa numbering; check against the edition the key uses before printing a verse number)
items.register: FACT for the grammar; TRADITION for the optional quotation.

items.verdict: UNIDIOMATIC. 'Makes sleep' reads as a modern paraphrase. I found no classical example of निद्रां करोति meaning 'sleeps'. A Monier-Williams English–Sanskrit listing reportedly has निद्रां कृ, but I could not check it. Replace it.
items.evidence: The classical verbs for 'sleeps' are स्वपिति (√स्वप्, class 2, stem with -i-; class-2 status confirmed by Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha word analyses and standard verb lists) and निद्राति (नि + √द्रा, 'to fall asleep, sleep'; MW nidrā 2 has -drāti). निद्रा (f.) 'sleep' is itself fine (MW).
items.course_wording: एकः सिंहः वने स्वपिति। (a whole word, with one honest line like the one for शृणोति/जानाति: its stem is built differently). Easier option: एकः सिंहः वने सुप्तः अस्ति। ('lies asleep'; a participle used as an adjective, like क्रुद्धः, बद्धः and मुक्तः later in the story).

items.verdict: CORRECT
items.evidence: उपरि takes the genitive by Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.30 षष्ठ्यतसर्थप्रत्ययेन, because उपरि (from 5.3.31) counts as an atas-sense form (avg-sanskrit.org; sanskritdocuments.org). √धाव् 'run' is class 1: धावति.
items.course_wording: एकः मूषकः सिंहस्य उपरि धावति। (teach सिंहस्य उपरि as a whole-word chunk, 'over the lion')

items.item: 12. सिंहः क्रुद्धः भवति। (the 1.x text has a gap: the lion never catches the mouse)
items.verdict: CORRECT. Adding a line is optional.
items.evidence: क्रुद्ध is the past participle of √क्रुध् 'be angry'.
items.course_wording: सिंहः क्रुद्धः भवति। सः मूषकम् गृह्णाति। (optional; गृह्णाति 'seizes' is a class-9 verb, glossed whole)

items.item: 13. मूषकः वदति — "माम् मुञ्च! अहम् तव साहाय्यम् करिष्यामि।"
items.verdict: THE FORMS ARE CORRECT, BUT करिष्यामि IS A FUTURE TENSE and falls outside a present-only toolkit. मुञ्च is an imperative (command), which can be taught as a chunk, as the course already does with वदतु and ददातु.
items.evidence: मुञ्च is the imperative 2nd singular of √मुच्. The root is tudādi and takes a nasal by Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.59 शे मुचादीनाम् (the Bhāgavata form मुञ्च is discussed at avg-sanskrit.org). करिष्यामि is the 1st singular simple future of √कृ. साहाय्यम् + कृ means 'give assistance' (Wiktionary, citing MW 1899: sāhāyyaṃ √kṛ). The present tense may stand for the future only when the time is near: Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.131 वर्तमानसामीप्ये वर्तमानवद्वा (sanskritdocuments.org). So करोमि as an open-ended promise would be weak. Classical quotations usually end with इति, which is optional in modern punctuated texts.
items.course_wording: Option A (recommended): माम् मुञ्च! अहम् कदाचित् तव साहाय्यम् करिष्यामि। Gloss करिष्यामि whole as 'I will do (future form, taught in Volume 3)', and कदाचित् as 'some day'. Option B (present tense only): माम् मुञ्च! अहम् अपि तव मित्रम्। ('Let me go! I too am your friend.'), and move the promise to the rescue scene, where a present for the near future is correct: अहम् जालम् कृन्तामि। ('I'll cut the net.' The UP Board Class 3 reader glosses कृन्तामि this same way.)

items.item: 14. A plot gap in 1.x: the lion never lets the mouse go
items.verdict: ADD TWO LINES
items.evidence: In every Aesopic and Demotic version, the lion lets the mouse go, often laughing at the idea of a mouse helping. मुञ्चति is the present of √मुच् with the same 7.1.59 nasal, and हसति is in the 10-verb bank.
items.course_wording: सिंहः हसति। सः मूषकम् मुञ्चति।

items.verdict: CORRECT
items.evidence: एकदा 'once, one day' is a standard narrative adverb; Pāli and Marathi cognate entries were confirmed, but the MW Sanskrit entry was not retrieved online in this session. जाल (n.) means 'net'. बद्ध is the past participle of √बन्ध्. To give the mouse a reason to come, add a roar: गर्जति (√गर्ज्, class 1, 'roars'). शृणोति and आगच्छति are already taught.
items.course_wording: एकदा सिंहः जाले बद्धः भवति। (or एकदा सिंहः जाले पतति।) सः गर्जति। मूषकः शृणोति। सः आगच्छति।

items.item: 16. मूषकः जालम् कर्तयति। (Is कर्तयति right, or should it be कृन्तति?)
items.verdict: WRONG IN CLASSICAL SANSKRIT. Use कृन्तति. कर्तयति is the causative ('causes to cut'). It does appear in modern spoken Sanskrit for 'cuts (with scissors)', so if it is ever mentioned it must be labelled modern.
items.evidence: The root for 'cut' is कृती छेदने, tudādi (class 6), in the mucādi subgroup (avg-sanskrit.org: 'कृतीँ छेदने #६'). That subgroup inserts a nasal before the class-6 suffix by Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.59 शे मुचादीनाम्, and the Kāśikā's examples include कृन्तति (sanskritdocuments.org 7.1.59). Kosha (from MW/Apte) gives कृत् with 6 P. कृन्तति 'to cut', and MW s.v. ut-kṛt gives -kṛntati. MW s.v. ni-kṛt gives 'Caus. -kartayati, to cause to cut' (Śāṅkhāyana Śrautasūtra), so कर्तयति is the causative. Modern spoken usage: kosha.sanskrit.today has 'सौचिकः कर्तर्या वस्त्रं कर्तयति'. School practice: the UP Board Class 3 'लघुः अपि सहायकः' uses कृन्तामि. (The class-10 root कृत 'mention, praise' gives कीर्तयति, not कर्तयति.)
items.course_wording: मूषकः जालम् कृन्तति। (gloss: 'gnaws through / cuts'). Teaching hook: कृन्तति and मुञ्चति get their nasal from the same rule.
items.ref: [REF:ashtadhyayi 7.1.59]; [REF:kashika 7.1.59]; [REF:dhatupatha tudādi कृती छेदने]; [REF:monierwilliams1899 s.v. kṛt, ni-kṛt]; [REF:apte1890 s.v. कृत्]
items.register: FACT, plus a usage label ('modern') if कर्तयति is mentioned.

items.verdict: CORRECT

items.item: 18. The lion story's moral: न कः अपि लघुः (1.x printed न कोऽपि लघुः)
items.verdict: CORRECT. Both spellings are the same sentence: one with the words joined by sandhi, one in pause form.
items.evidence: कोऽपि = कः + अपि: before a, the visarga turns the preceding a into o, and the lost a is shown by the avagraha sign ऽ. The pause-form spelling कः अपि follows the course policy, but learners should be told that printed texts almost always show कोऽपि. लघु means 'light, small, insignificant' (MW laghu). The moral matches the standard Aesopic one (Wikipedia: 'no being so small that it cannot help a greater'). A positive version echoes the UP Board lesson title 'लघुः अपि सहायकः'.
items.course_wording: न कः अपि लघुः। (joined form: न कोऽपि लघुः — 'No one is too small.') Alternative: लघुः अपि सहायकः भवति। ('Even a small one becomes a helper.')

I changed no repo files.

1. **Limits of this check.** curl and WebFetch were blocked for Wikipedia, Wikisource, GRETIL, sanskritdocuments, the Cologne/Apte dictionaries, wisdomlib and archive.org. Every verdict therefore rests on WebSearch result snippets. Before Pass C signs off, re-check the dictionary entries marked as not retrieved in item 19, and the Lichtheim page range.

2. **Possible problem with the `panchatantra` key.** REFERENCES.md says "Textus simplicior unless noted; Tr.: Olivelle 1997". But publisher descriptions of Olivelle's Oxford World's Classics volume say it involves Franklin Edgerton's reconstruction of the original text. If that translation follows Edgerton rather than the textus simplicior, the key mixes two texts; a maintainer should confirm and fix the entry. In any case, the mice-and-elephants story is verified only in Pūrṇabhadra's recension (Ryder 1925), so cite it with the recension named.

3. **Facts I could not settle.**
   - The Babrius fable number for the lion and the mouse: left out.
   - The Avianus fable number (I believe 27): left out of the course wording.
   - The Greek Anthology number for Bianor's poem: not checked.
   - The Pañcatantra locus of "बुद्धिर्यस्य बलं तस्य": verified only as Hitopadeśa 2.122, in one online edition's numbering.
   - Whether MW records श्रेष्� with an ablative: not retrieved, so item 9 is hedged.
   - NCERT use of either story: not confirmed. The UP Board Sanskrit readers are confirmed (Class 5 'काकस्य उद्यमः'; Class 3 'लघुः अपि सहायकः', which uses कृन्तामि).

4. **Claims to keep out of the course.**
   - "The Thirsty Crow is a Pañcatantra story."
   - "A Lothal jar shows the thirsty crow."
   - "Aesop copied the Hitopadeśa", or the reverse.

   None of these is on the banned list in EDITORIAL_GUIDELINES §3. Consider adding the first two as documented errors.

5. **New REFERENCES entries needed.** Full entries are given inside items 1–3: perry1952, duff1934 (Avianus), rackham1940 (Pliny NH 10.125), lichtheim1980 and ryder1925. All verdicts should be logged in research/verification-log.md as EDITORIAL_GUIDELINES §2.5 requires.

corrections.item: 1. Thirsty Crow, HISTORY callout: "This story does not come from ancient India."
corrections.problem: Overclaimed. What the evidence shows is that no ancient Indian text has the story and that the earliest surviving versions are Greek and Latin. It does not prove where the story began. The claim also clashes with item 1b: a published reading of a Harappan jar from Lothal, attributed to the archaeologist B.B. Lal, is in wide circulation in India, so a flat denial invites challenge.
corrections.corrected_wording: No ancient Indian text tells this story. Its earliest known versions are Greek and Latin, from the Aesopic tradition: 'The Crow and the Pitcher' (no. 390 in B.E. Perry's catalogue of Aesop's fables).

corrections.item: 1. Thirsty Crow, HISTORY callout: "It first appears in a Greek poem by Bianor (1st century CE) and in the Latin fables of Avianus (around 400 CE)"
corrections.problem: Wrong as written. Avianus (c. 400 CE) is not a first appearance: Pliny (77 CE) and pseudo-Dositheus (2nd c.) are both earlier. For Bianor, 'first appears' is stronger than the sources allow; they support only 'earliest known/dated'.
corrections.corrected_wording: The earliest known version is a short Greek poem by Bianor (1st century CE). The best-known ancient telling is in the Latin verse fables of Avianus (around 400 CE), whose moral is that cleverness beats brute strength.

corrections.item: 1. Thirsty Crow, HISTORY callout: "Pliny the Elder reports the same trick as something a real crow was seen doing."
corrections.problem: Overclaimed twice over. (a) Pliny's bird appears in his discussion of ravens (corvus). Rackham's Loeb translation and Holland's both render it 'raven'; only Bostock–Riley says 'crow'. (b) Pliny does not vouch for the sighting. He passes it on as something 'certain persons have thought worth recording' (NH 10.125).
corrections.corrected_wording: Pliny the Elder (1st century CE) passes on a report that a real raven once did the same thing.

corrections.item: 1. Thirsty Crow, Teacher Note: "no Sanskrit text of the Pañcatantra contains this fable"
corrections.problem: Under-hedged. This is a universal negative across dozens of recensions and versions, most of which no one has searched for this story. The research supports only 'no known version'.
corrections.corrected_wording: Some books call it 'a Pañcatantra story'. That label is modern. No known version of the Pañcatantra or the Hitopadeśa, and no Jātaka, contains this fable.

corrections.item: 1b. Lothal jar: the course wording "Some popular writers read a painted jar from Lothal as this story, but archaeologists have not established that reading", and the suggestion to list it as a 'documented error'
corrections.problem: Inaccurate attribution, and it overclaims in the opposite direction. The thirsty-crow reading of a small painted Lothal vase (crow, pot and deer) is not only popular. Secondary sources attribute it to the archaeologist B.B. Lal (a 2025 IJFMR paper credits the figure to Lal 2002, presumably *The Sarasvati Flows On*; a UPSC study note says 'B.B. Lal has identified on a vase a painting probably depicting the tale "the thirsty crow"'). It is also a standard answer in Indian competitive-exam quiz banks ('A vase depicting the folk tale The Thirsty Crow was found at: Lothal'), so teachers and learners are likely to meet it. It is a contested interpretation of an image with no text. Listing it as a 'documented error' would itself be an overclaim.
corrections.corrected_wording: Teacher Note: "A small painted vase from the Harappan site of Lothal shows a bird, a pot and a deer. Some archaeologists, notably B.B. Lal, and many Indian exam guides read it as the thirsty-crow story. A picture without words cannot show which story was meant, so the reading is not established, and the course does not teach it." List it as a 'contested interpretation', not a 'documented error', and verify the Lal 2002 locus before naming him in print.

corrections.item: 2. Lion and Mouse, HISTORY callout: "in one version of the Pañcatantra, mice repay a herd of elephants by gnawing them free from hunters' nets"
corrections.problem: A detail is wrong. In Pūrṇabhadra's recension (Ryder 1925, 'The Mice That Set Elephants Free'), a king's elephant-trappers catch the herd in a water-trap and tie the elephants to trees with ropes. The mice gnaw through the ropes ('gnawed the guy-ropes where they stood ... by cutting the ropes aloft, set their friends free'). Nets appear only in modern retellings. The vague phrase 'one version' should also name the recension, as item 3 requires.
corrections.corrected_wording: India's own fable books have a cousin of it: in Pūrṇabhadra's version of the Pañcatantra (1199 CE), mice repay a herd of elephants by gnawing through the ropes that tied them to trees after a king's trappers caught them.

corrections.item: 3. Mice freeing elephants: the locus verdict ("told by the deer Citrāṅga ... during the episode of his capture in a snare") and the course wording "caught in hunters' nets"
corrections.problem: The narrative context is wrong. In Ryder's Book II, Spot (Citrāṅga) tells the story when he first comes to the friends and asks to join them. The turtle Slow (Mantharaka) has objected that such small creatures are no match as friends for a big animal. Spot answers that the small can matter, quotes 'Make friends, make friends...', Slow asks 'How was that?', and Spot tells the tale. It is not told during his capture in a snare; 'Spot's Captivity' is a separate story that follows. The course wording repeats the 'nets' error from item 2.
corrections.corrected_wording: "In Pūrṇabhadra's version of the Pañcatantra (1199 CE), in Book 2, 'Winning Friends', the deer Citrāṅga asks to join the mouse, the crow and the turtle. To show that small creatures make worthy friends, he tells how mice once freed a herd of elephants by gnawing through the ropes that tied them to trees after a king's trappers caught them." Keep the rest of the item's caveats: no story or verse number, and textus simplicior, Edgerton and Olivelle unverified.

corrections.item: 9. Crow moral बुद्धिः बलात् श्रेष्ठा: the verdict "NOT THE TEXTBOOK CLASSICAL CONSTRUCTION ... The pattern 'X से श्रेष्ठ' is Hindi ... treat श्रेष्ठा + ablative as non-standard"
corrections.problem: Overclaimed. Monier-Williams s.v. śreṣṭha records the sense 'better than' with the ablative or genitive (citing Manu and the Mahābhārata, as reproduced in the online mirrors), and Apte gives a similar gloss. Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.42 पञ्चमी विभक्ते depends on a two-way distinction (vibhāga), not on a -tara suffix, and the researcher's own Whitney §292b citation covers 'words used in a comparative sense'. The sentence is grammatical classical Sanskrit, and calling it a Hindi calque is unsupported. श्रेयसी is a reasonable stylistic choice, not a correction.
corrections.corrected_wording: Verdict: CORRECT. बुद्धिः बलात् श्रेष्ठा। is grammatical: śreṣṭha 'better than' takes the ablative (MW, Apte; Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.42). Optional alternative with the comparative proper: बुद्धिः बलात् श्रेयसी। Either may be printed; if the course switches, present the change as a style choice, not an error fix.

corrections.item: 16 (and the echo in 19). कर्तयति: the verdict "WRONG IN CLASSICAL SANSKRIT ... must be labelled modern"
corrections.problem: Overclaimed. Monier-Williams s.v. kṛt gives 'Caus. kartayati, id.' (the same sense, 'to cut') and cites the Pañcatantra. The form is causative in shape but is attested in classical narrative prose in the plain sense 'cuts'. It is not merely modern spoken usage, and it is not wrong. कृन्तति remains the basic class-6 present and the better teaching choice, and the 7.1.59 teaching hook stands.
corrections.corrected_wording: Verdict: PREFER कृन्तति. कर्तयति is formally the causative of √कृत्. It is also used in the plain sense 'cuts' (MW s.v. kṛt: 'Caus. kartayati, id.', Pañcatantra) and in modern spoken Sanskrit, but the basic present is कृन्तति. Course wording: मूषकः जालम् कृन्तति। If कर्तयति is mentioned, label it 'causative form, also used for "cuts"', not 'modern'. In item 19, change 'All correct except two: कर्तयति (should be कृन्तति)' to 'कर्तयति replaced by the more basic कृन्तति'.

corrections.item: 18. Sandhi explanation for कोऽपि: "before a, the visarga turns the preceding a into o"
corrections.problem: This misdescribes the rule, and the text may be copied into the lesson. The visarga does not change the preceding a while itself remaining: the whole ending -aḥ becomes -o before a-, and the initial a- of the next word drops, which the avagraha ऽ marks.
corrections.corrected_wording: कोऽपि = कः + अपि: before a word beginning with अ, the ending -अः becomes -ओ, and the अ of the next word drops out; the avagraha ऽ marks where it was.

corrections.item: 20. Evidence line: "Forms that are not nominative are glossed as whole words: ... बलात्, श्रेयसी"
corrections.problem: श्रेयसी is a nominative (feminine singular, agreeing with बुद्धिः). It is glossed whole because the comparative -īyas stem and its feminine are outside the toolkit, not because of its case.
corrections.corrected_wording: Forms glossed as whole words: घटम्, घटे, पाषाणम्, जलम् (object) and बलात>, which are not nominative, and श्रेयसी, a nominative feminine of a comparative stem not yet taught.

check.overall:
Most items hold up: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17 and 21, plus the reference keys and the repo ledger claims (पुनः, अल्पम्, आगच्छति, हसति, वदतु, ददातु). Eleven entries need correcting.

Two changes matter most:
- **Story history (items 1, 1b, 2, 3).** The thirsty-crow callout states a flat 'does not come from ancient India', misdates Avianus as a 'first appearance', and turns Pliny's hearsay raven into a 'crow seen doing it'. The Lothal reading is attributed to the archaeologist B.B. Lal and is a stock Indian exam answer, so 'popular writers' is inaccurate and it should not be listed as a documented error. The Pañcatantra mice-and-elephants story uses a trap and ropes tied to trees, not 'hunters' nets'. The deer tells it when he first asks to join the friends, not during his snare capture.
- **Two grammar verdicts are overclaimed.** MW and Apte record śreṣṭha 'better than' with the ablative, so बुद्धिः बलात् श्रेष्ठा is grammatical classical Sanskrit (item 9). MW s.v. kṛt has 'Caus. kartayati, id.' citing the Pañcatantra, so कर्तयति is not 'wrong' or merely modern (item 16), though कृन्तति remains the better teaching choice.

Minor fixes: the avagraha sandhi description (item 18) and calling श्रेयसी non-nominative (item 20).

Limits: WebFetch and curl were blocked for nearly every host (Wikisource, wisdomlib, kosha, attalus, Perseus mirrors). All checks rest on WebSearch snippets, so the MW entries for śreṣṭha and kṛt and the Lal 2002 attribution should be confirmed against the printed sources before publication. No files were edited.

items.item: 1a. अहिंसा परमो धर्मः: where it occurs in the Mahābhārata (Ādiparvan 11.13? Anuśāsana 115/116?)
items.verdict: VERIFIED, with corrected numbering. In the critical-edition (CE) main text the exact phrase occurs 5 times: 1.11.12, 3.198.69, 13.116.1, 13.116.25 and 13.117.37. '1.11.13' is the number some non-critical editions use for the Ādiparvan line. 'Anuśāsana 115/116' are older chapter numbers for the 13.116–117 passages, so cite CE numbers. Context: (i) 1.11.12, Pauloma section: the sage Sahasrapād (1.10.7) has been cursed into a harmless ḍuṇḍubha snake. Freed from that body, he teaches Ruru, who had vowed to kill every snake after one bit his bride (1.10.1–2). The verse continues सर्वप्राणभृतां स्मृतः / तस्मात् प्राणभृतः सर्वान् न हिंस्याद् ब्राह्मणः क्व चित्. 1.11.14–15 then set this brahmin dharma against the kṣatriya's dharma of wielding the rod (daṇḍadhāraṇa) and protecting subjects. (ii) 3.198.69: the righteous hunter (vyādha) teaching a brahmin; it continues 'sa ca satye pratiṣṭhitaḥ'. (iii) 13.116.1: Yudhiṣṭhira quotes Bhīṣma. 13.116.25 continues 'tathāhiṃsā paraṃ tapaḥ'. 13.117.37 is Bhīṣma's chain 'ahiṃsā paramo dharmas tathāhiṃsā paro damaḥ / ahiṃsā paramaṃ dānam ahiṃsā paramaṃ tapaḥ', followed by 13.117.38 'ahiṃsā paramo yajñaḥ…'. Both chapters discuss abstaining from meat.

items.course_wording:
> **[TRADITION · परम्परा]** The Mahābhārata uses the line अहिंसा परमो धर्मः (ahiṃsā paramo dharmaḥ), "non-harming is the highest dharma," several times. At its first appearance (Ādiparvan 1.11.12 in the critical edition) a sage freed from a snake's body speaks to the young brahmin Ruru, who has sworn to kill every snake: अहिंसा परमो धर्मः सर्वप्राणभृतां स्मृतः, "non-harming is held to be the highest dharma of all living beings," and so a brahmin should never harm any creature. The next verses set this against the warrior's duty of wielding the rod of punishment. Later, Bhīṣma repeats the line in a chain of praises: अहिंसा परमो धर्मस्तथाहिंसा परो दमः … (13.117.37). [REF:mahabharata 1.11.12]; [REF:mahabharata 13.117.37]

items.verdict: NOT IN THE MAHĀBHĀRATA as critically edited: zero hits. At every locus the verse goes on differently. 1.11.12 has 'sarvaprāṇabhṛtāṃ smṛtaḥ'. 3.198.69 has 'sa ca satye pratiṣṭhitaḥ'. 13.116.25 has 'tathāhiṃsā paraṃ tapaḥ'. 13.117.37 has 'tathāhiṃsā paro damaḥ'. The line is also absent from the star passages and Appendix-I passages in the GRETIL e-text, and from every other GRETIL Sanskrit text I searched (about 3,400 files, including Purāṇas, subhāṣita collections and narrative literature) and the DCS Purāṇas. No one who quotes the line gives a working locus; the most common claim is 'Anuśāsana 116', where the text actually reads 'tathāhiṃsā paro damaḥ'. I could not find out where or when the line started, so say "no source found", not who invented it. Limits of the check: the e-text does not include the CE's apparatus of single-word variant readings, and I could not open Gita Press or other vulgate editions directly. The closest real passage is CE Anuśāsana App. I no. 15, lines 1203–1205, which is outside the main text. It condemns retainers who say 'ahiṃsā paramo dharmaḥ' and refuse to fight in battle.
items.evidence: Local regex searches of the CE e-text, both copies (GRETIL mirror and DharmicData/sacred-texts): no 'dharmahiṃsā', 'dharma hiṃsā' or 'hiṃsā tathaiva'. The whole GRETIL 1_sanskr checkout and the DCS Purāṇa files (https://github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit) also gave zero hits. Web: an Advaita-L thread calls it fake, and a challenge there to show the verse goes unanswered (https://www.advaita-vedanta.org/archives/advaita-l/2019-April/052024.html, https://lists.advaita-vedanta.org/archives/advaita-l/2019-April/052028.html). Acharya Prashant, https://acharyaprashant.org/en/articles/anhinsaa-paramo-dharmh-galat-hai-hinsaa-hi-dharm-hai-1_9365009, and booksfact, https://www.booksfact.com/puranas/ahimsa-paramo-dharmah-dharma-himsa-tathaiva-cha-sloka.html, also say it is not in the text. Sites that present it as genuine give no edition-level locus: Bharata Bharati / Chinmayananda https://bharatabharati.in/2011/07/15/dharma-himsa-tathaiva-cha-swami-chinmayananda/; Hindupedia https://hindupedia.com/en/Ahimsa_Paramo_Dharma; Brainly/YouTube ('Anuśāsana 116'). None of these is scholarly, which is why the verdict rests on the CE search above.

items.item: 2a. उद्यमेन हि सिध्यन्ति कार्याणि न मनोरथैः। न हि सुप्तस्य सिंहस्य प्रविशन्ति मुखे मृगाः॥: source
items.verdict: VERIFIED: Hitopadeśa, introduction (prastāvikā; the kathāmukha frame story), verse 36. GRETIL numbers it Hit_0.36 and Apte cites it twice as 'H. Pr. 36'. In the story King Sudarśana of Pāṭaliputra, troubled that his sons will not study, reflects on fate and effort (0.30–36). Then he convenes the learned and Viṣṇuśarman takes the princes on. It is NOT in Mitralābha, although one blog says so. The verse also appears in the Pañcatantra, tantra 2 (Mitrasaṃprāpti, story of Somilaka the weaver), with a variant last quarter 'na hi suptasya siṃhasya viśanti vadane mṛgāḥ'. That is 2.136 in the GRETIL e-text of R. Jha's edition, and Apte cites it as 'Pt. 2.131', so numbering differs by edition. The Hitopadeśa says it draws on the Pañcatantra (Hit 0.9), which explains the shared verse. The lion half-line also circulates with other first lines (Sternbach MSS 6887, 6890, 6911).
items.evidence: GRETIL hitop_u.htm (input Jan Brzezinski, revised Ulrich Stiehl): 'udyamena hi sidhyanti kāryāṇi na manorathaiḥ | nahi suptasya siṃhasya praviśanti mukhe mṛgāḥ // Hit_0.36 //'. DCS Hitopadeśa places the same line in section 'Hitop, 0' (https://github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit). GRETIL vispancu.htm (Jha ed., Chowkhamba 1991; Kale ed. consulted) gives Panc_2.136. Apte 1890 s.v. सिध् quotes 'udyamena hi sidhyanti kāryāṇi na manorathaiḥ H. Pr. 36'; s.v. सुप्त, 'na hi suptasya siṃhasya praviśanti mukhe mṛgāḥ H. Pr. 36'; s.v. उद्यमः, the same line as 'Pt. 2.131' (Cologne csl-orig ap90.txt, https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-orig). The GRETIL file msubhs_u.htm has MSS 6888 with this exact text. Web: IGNCA PDF https://ignca.gov.in/sanskrit/hitopadesa.pdf and https://brah.ma/shlok/udyamena-hi-sidhyanti-kaaryaani-na-manorathaih both put it at 36 in the opening section. https://blog.practicalsanskrit.com/2010/02/no-substitute-for-hard-work.html says 'mitralābha', which is wrong.

> **[TRADITION · परम्परा]** The Hitopadeśa (introduction, verse 36 in common editions) has this verse, and it also appears in the Pañcatantra (Book 2): उद्यमेन हि सिध्यन्ति कार्याणि न मनोरथैः। न हि सुप्तस्य सिंहस्य प्रविशन्ति मुखे मृगाः॥ (udyamena hi sidhyanti kāryāṇi na manorathaiḥ / na hi suptasya siṃhasya praviśanti mukhe mṛgāḥ). It means: "Tasks succeed through effort, not through wishing; deer do not walk into the mouth of a sleeping lion." In the book's opening story, King Sudarśana thinks of it while worrying about his idle sons, just before he finds them a teacher. [REF:hitopadesha prastāvikā 36]; [REF:panchatantra tantra 2]

Source line for a caption: "Hitopadeśa, Prastāvikā 36 (also Pañcatantra, Book 2)".

items.item: 2b. Word-by-word glosses: उद्यमेन हि सिध्यन्ति कार्याणि न मनोरथैः। न हि सुप्तस्य सिंहस्य प्रविशन्ति मुखे मृगाः॥
items.verdict: VERIFIED against Apte 1890, which quotes this very verse under सिध्, सुप्त and उद्यम, and against Whitney for the case uses. मृग is generic in Apte: 1(a) 'a quadruped, an animal in general', 2 'a deer, an antelope', 3 'game'. So 'deer' is standard, and 'wild animals' is a defensible alternative. Spelling: teach सिध्यन्ति (√सिध्, class 4). Some printings show सिद्ध्यन्ति, an optional consonant doubling permitted by Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.4.47 अनचि च; it is not a different word.
items.evidence: Apte 1890 (csl-orig ap90.txt): उद्यमः 'strenuous or assiduous effort, exertion'; हि 'for, because… indeed, surely', never at the start of a sentence; सिध् (4P) 'to be accomplished or fulfilled'; कार्य 'what ought to be done… work, action'; मनस्, compound -रथः ''the car of the mind', a wish, desire'; सुप्त 'slept, sleeping, asleep'; सिंहः 'a lion'; प्रविश् (6P) 'to enter into'; मुखं 'the mouth'; मृगः as above. Whitney 1889 (text via https://github.com/vishvAsa/sanskrit, vyAkaraNam/whitney): §280 instrumental of means; §304 the 'pregnant' locative expressing the goal of motion (मुखे with प्रविशन्ति). Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.4.47 verified in https://github.com/ashtadhyayi-com/data.

Translation: "Tasks succeed through effort, not through wishing; deer do not walk into the mouth of a sleeping lion." items.item: 3a. अष्टादशपुराणेषु व्यासस्य वचनद्वयम्। परोपकारः पुण्याय पापाय परपीडनम्॥: actual source
items.verdict: FRAME NOT TRACED; SECOND LINE ATTESTED ELSEWHERE. (1) I could not trace the first line, 'aṣṭādaśapurāṇeṣu vyāsasya vacanadvayam', to any Purāṇa. Read literally, it is a summary *about* the Purāṇas: it mentions Vyāsa in the third person, so even by its own wording it does not claim to be Vyāsa's words. The full couplet is recorded as an anthology verse in Sternbach's Mahā-subhāṣita-saṃgraha, no. 3587. I could not see the source list for that entry. (2) The second line appears in the Pañcatantra, tantra 3 (Kākolūkīya; 3.103 in the GRETIL e-text of Jha's edition), in the tale of the hare and the partridge, under a different first line: 'saṅkṣepāt kathyate dharmo janāḥ kiṃ vistareṇa vaḥ'. The speaker is the cat Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra. He poses as an ascetic, preaches dharma and ahiṃsā, lures the two animals who came to him for judgment within reach, and eats them both. It is the same irony as the jackal behind वसुधैव कुटुम्बकम्. Apte quotes the line without giving a source. Searches came up empty in the Purāṇa e-texts I could reach: GRETIL and DCS copies of Agni, Bhāgavata, Brahma, Brahmāṇḍa, Garuḍa, Kālikā, Kūrma, Liṅga, Mārkaṇḍeya, Matsya, Nārada, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Viṣṇu, and parts of Śiva, Skanda, Varāha and Viṣṇudharmottara. I could not search Padma, Bhaviṣya, Brahmavaivarta, Vāyu or most of Skanda, so 'not found' is not proof that it is absent.
items.evidence: GRETIL vispancu.htm, kathā 2 'śaśa-kapiñjala-kathā' of tantra 3: 'saṅkṣepāt kathyate dharmo janāḥ kiṃ vistareṇa vaḥ | paropakāraḥ puṇyāya pāpāya para-pīḍanam ||Panc_3.103||', inside the cat's 'dharmopadeśanā'. GRETIL msubhs_u.htm has MSS_3587 with the full couplet (see also https://www.wisdomlib.org/sanskrit/quote/mss/subhashita-3587). Sternbach MSS bibliographic data: de Jong's review of vol. 1 (Hoshiarpur: VVRI 1974, Vishveshvaranand Indological Series 64), https://jainqq.org/explore/269283/4. Apte 1890 s.v. पर, compound -उपकारः, quotes 'paropakāraḥ puṇyāya pāpāya parapīḍanam' with no locus. A grep for 'vacanadvayam', 'puṇyāya pāpāya' and 'parapīḍan' across all of GRETIL 1_sanskr and the DCS Purāṇas found it only in MSS and the Pañcatantra. Popular pages give no Purāṇic locus: https://anusilana.in/astadasa-purane%E1%B9%A3u-vyasasya-vacana-dvayam/, https://www.quora.com/Can-you-explain-in-detail-the-Sanskrit-Shloka-Ashtadasha-puraneshu-Vyasasya-vachanam-dvayam-paropakaraha-punyaya-papaya-parapeedanam, http://subhaashitani.blogspot.com/2015/06/in-all-18-puranas-only-two-messages-of.html.
items.course_wording:
> **[TRADITION · परम्परा]** A popular verse sums up the eighteen Purāṇas as "two sayings of Vyāsa": अष्टादशपुराणेषु व्यासस्य वचनद्वयम्। परोपकारः पुण्याय पापाय परपीडनम्॥ (aṣṭādaśapurāṇeṣu vyāsasya vacanadvayam / paropakāraḥ puṇyāya pāpāya parapīḍanam). It means: "In the eighteen Purāṇas, Vyāsa says two things: helping others brings merit; harming others brings sin." Tradition credits the thought to Vyāsa, but the verse itself is a summary *about* the Purāṇas (notice that it speaks of Vyāsa as "he"), and it has not been traced to any Purāṇa. Its second line also appears in the Pañcatantra (Book 3, the tale of the hare and the partridge), with a different first line. As with वसुधैव कुटुम्बकम्, the speaker is a schemer: a cat posing as a holy man, who then eats both animals that came to him for judgment. [REF:panchatantra tantra 3]; [REF:sternbach1974 3587]

Source line for a caption: "Traditional verse (anthologized; source untraced). Second line also in Pañcatantra, Book 3."
items.register: TRADITION ("traditionally ascribed"; never quiz the Vyāsa attribution as fact). An "According to the Pañcatantra…" item about the cat is allowed.
items.ref: [REF:panchatantra tantra 3] (same Olivelle-translation caveat as 2a); [REF:apte1890 s.v. पर] for the line's currency. Sternbach has no key yet. Needs a new REFERENCES entry: sternbach1974 — L. Sternbach (ed.), *Mahā-subhāṣita-saṃgraha*, Hoshiarpur: Vishveshvaranand Vedic Research Institute, 1974– (Vishveshvaranand Indological Series 64 ff.). Cited by subhāṣita number (e.g. 3587).

items.item: 3b. Word-by-word glosses: अष्टादशपुराणेषु व्यासस्य वचनद्वयम्। परोपकारः पुण्याय पापाय परपीडनम्॥
items.verdict: VERIFIED against Apte 1890 and Whitney. Neither line has a verb; English supplies "there are" and "leads to". पुण्याय and पापाय are datives of purpose (Whitney §287). Pass A note: Sanskrit पीडनम् is written with plain ड. Do not carry over the Hindi nukta spelling (पीड़ा).
items.evidence: Apte 1890: अष्टन् in compounds gives अष्टादशन् 'eighteen'; पुराण 'a tale of the past, legend…'; व्यासः 'N. of a celebrated sage'; वचनं 'speech, an utterance… a text, dictum'; द्वयं 'pair, couple, usually at the end of a compound'; पर, compound -उपकारः 'doing good to others, benevolence' (Apte quotes this line here); पुण्यं 'virtue, religious or moral merit'; पापं 'evil… sin'; पीडनं 'paining, distressing, oppressing'. Whitney §287 (dative of end or purpose) checked in the vishvAsa/sanskrit copy.
items.course_wording: अष्टादश (aṣṭādaśa) "eighteen" · पुराणेषु (purāṇeṣu) "in the Purāṇas" · व्यासस्य (vyāsasya) "of Vyāsa" · वचनद्वयम् (vacanadvayam) "a pair of sayings": वचन "saying" + द्वय "pair" · परोपकारः (paropakāraḥ) "helping others": पर "other" + उपकारः "help" · पुण्याय (puṇyāya) "for merit" · पापाय (pāpāya) "for sin" · परपीडनम् (parapīḍanam) "harming others": पर + पीडनम् "causing pain". Translation: "In the eighteen Purāṇas, Vyāsa says two things: helping others brings merit; harming others brings sin." [REF:apte1890 s.v. पर]; [REF:apte1890 s.v. पीडन]; [REF:whitney1889 §287]

items.item: 1c. Glosses for अहिंसा परमो धर्मः (resolved: अहिंसा परमः धर्मः)
items.verdict: VERIFIED. This is a nominal sentence: Sanskrit leaves 'is' unsaid. परमः is masculine because it agrees with धर्मः; it does not describe the feminine अहिंसा. The genitive in the Ādiparvan continuation (सर्वप्राणभृतां) can be read as 'for all living beings' or 'toward all living beings'; English 'of all living beings' keeps that ambiguity.
items.evidence: Apte 1890 (csl-orig): अहिंसा 'harmlessness, abstaining from killing or giving pain to others in thought, word, or deed; as ahiṃsā paramo dharmaḥ'; परम 'highest, best… chief, supreme'; धर्मः 'religion… law, usage… religious or moral merit… duty'.
items.course_wording: अहिंसा (ahiṃsā) "non-harming, non-violence": अ- "not" + हिंसा "harm" · परमः (paramaḥ) "highest, supreme" · धर्मः (dharmaḥ) "duty, right conduct, law". There is no word for "is": Sanskrit leaves it unsaid. परमः is masculine because it describes धर्मः. Translation: "Non-harming is the highest dharma." [REF:apte1890 s.v. अहिंसा]; [REF:apte1890 s.v. परम]

items.item: 4. Sandhi joins present (one line each), for the resolved display plus the labelled 'joined original' preview
items.verdict: VERIFIED. Saying 1 has exactly one join between words: परमः + धर्मः → परमो धर्मः. Sayings 2 and 3 have NO joins between words: the printed verses are already in pause form, so their 'joined original' preview is identical except that some editions print न हि as नहि. They do contain joins inside compounds: मनोरथ- (मनस् + रथ, the same -as → -o rule) and परोपकारः (पर + उपकारः, a + u → o). If the Bhīṣma line is shown: धर्मस्तथाहिंसा ← धर्मः तथा अहिंसा (visarga → s before t; ā + a → ā). If the Pañcatantra frame line is shown: धर्मो जनाः ← धर्मः जनाः (the same rule as परमो). Visarga before प stays a visarga in परोपकारः पुण्याय.
items.evidence: Whitney 1889, checked in the vishvAsa/sanskrit copy: §175a 'Final as, before any sonant consonant and before short a, is changed to o'; §170b s is retained before t; §170d before p it becomes visarga in practice; §126 two a-vowels give ā; §127 a + u-vowel gives o. Aṣṭādhyāyī sūtra texts checked in ashtadhyayi-com/data: 8.2.66 ससजुषो रुः; 6.1.113 अतो रोरप्लुतादप्लुते; 6.1.114 हशि च; 6.1.87 आद्गुणः; 6.1.101 अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः; 8.3.15 खरवसानयोर्विसर्जनीयः; 8.3.34 विसर्जनीयस्य सः.
items.course_wording:
परमो ← परमः: before a voiced consonant (here ध्), a final -अः becomes -ओ: परमः + धर्मः → परमो धर्मः. [REF:whitney1889 §175]; [REF:ashtadhyayi 6.1.114]
मनोरथैः is one word, not a join between words: मनस् "mind" + रथ "chariot", fused by the same -as → -o change. Learn it whole as मनोरथ "wish". [REF:whitney1889 §175]; [REF:apte1890 s.v. मनस्]
परोपकारः is one word: पर "other" + उपकारः "help"; अ + उ → ओ. [REF:whitney1889 §127]; [REF:ashtadhyayi 6.1.87]
Sayings 2 and 3 have no joins between words: what you read is already the pause form (some editions print न हि as नहि).
(Only if the Bhīṣma line is shown:) धर्मस्तथाहिंसा ← धर्मः तथा अहिंसा: visarga becomes स् before त्, and आ + अ → आ. [REF:whitney1889 §170]; [REF:whitney1889 §126]

- The Anuśāsana loci are critical-edition 13.116.1, 13.116.25 and 13.117.37; 13.117.38 is the 'paramo yajñaḥ' continuation. '115/116' are vulgate chapter numbers.

Verse numbers in the Pañcatantra GRETIL e-text (Jha ed.: 2.136, 3.103) differ from Apte's 'Pt. 2.131', so cite by tantra only, as the repo already does ([REF:panchatantra tantra 3]).

Optional Teacher Notes, all verified in the e-texts:
(a) The epic calls several things the highest dharma. For example, ānṛśaṃsyaṃ paro dharmaḥ ('non-cruelty is the highest dharma') occurs 8 times in the critical edition's main text (e.g. 3.203.41, 12.316.12). So learners should not read अहिंसा परमो धर्मः as the epic's single motto.

corrections.item: 1a (and 1c). Ādiparvan locus: the '1.11.13 is just another edition's number' explanation
corrections.problem: Under-described. The difference is in the wording as well as the number. The popular vulgate text that numbers the line 1.11.13 (vedapath.app 1.11.13) reads it as the second half of a verse that opens इदं चोवाच वचनं रुरुमप्रतिमौजसम् (= CE star passage *241_03), and ends अहिंसा परमो धर्मः सर्वप्राणभृतां वर. The last word is a vocative: "O best of all living beings", addressed to Ruru. It does not have the CE's स्मृतः. Ganguli, who translates the vulgate, matches this: "O thou first of created beings, verily the highest virtue of man is sparing the life of others" (Ādi Section XI). So learners who check Ganguli, Gita Press-type texts or vedapath will find a different line and a different translation. The 1c note that the genitive is ambiguous ('for/toward all beings') holds only for the CE reading. I confirmed the CE text and numbering myself (GRETIL mbh_01_u.htm: 01,011.012a ... sarvaprāṇabhṛtāṃ smṛtaḥ; star passages *0240–*0242 come just before it). The vulgate reading rests on two independent web sources (the vedapath snippet and Ganguli's wording). I could not open a printed vulgate.
corrections.corrected_wording: Verdict: "1.11.12 in the critical edition. Vulgate editions number the passage 1.11.13 and read its second half differently: अहिंसा परमो धर्मः सर्वप्राणभृतां वर, 'non-harming is the highest dharma, O best of all living beings' (a vocative addressed to Ruru; cf. Ganguli, Ādi Section XI). The course quotes and translates the critical-edition reading." Teacher Notes line: "If students find 'सर्वप्राणभृतां वर' or 'O thou first of created beings', that is the vulgate reading of the same line (numbered 1.11.13 there). The course follows the critical edition's सर्वप्राणभृतां स्मृतः." In 1c, add: "(this applies to the critical-edition reading; in the vulgate the genitive depends on वर, 'best of all living beings')."

corrections.item: 4. Sandhi joins present: 'Saying 1 has exactly one join between words'
corrections.problem: Incomplete for what the lesson actually shows. The bare saying has one join, but the 1a callout prints the full Ādiparvan line अहिंसा परमो धर्मः सर्वप्राणभृतां स्मृतः. That line has a second external join: सर्वप्राणभृताम् + स्मृतः → सर्वप्राणभृतां स्मृतः (final म् becomes anusvāra before a sibilant). Sources: Whitney §213e, checked in the vishvAsa copy; Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.23 मोऽनुस्वारः, checked in ashtadhyayi-com data. Item 4 also gives no line for it.
corrections.corrected_wording: Add: "(For the full Ādiparvan line shown in the callout:) सर्वप्राणभृतां स्मृतः ← सर्वप्राणभृताम् स्मृतः: a final म् becomes anusvāra (ं) before a consonant such as स्. [REF:whitney1889 §213]; [REF:ashtadhyayi 8.3.23]". Change the claim to: "The three-word saying has exactly one join (परमो ← परमः); the full Ādiparvan line adds a second (-ां ← -ाम् before स्)."

corrections.item: 2a and 3a. Pañcatantra citations ([REF:panchatantra tantra 2], [REF:panchatantra tantra 3]) and the course wording 'it also appears in the Pañcatantra'
corrections.problem: The open caveat can now be settled, and it goes against the citation. Olivelle 1997 (OUP; Oxford World's Classics) translates Franklin Edgerton's 1924 reconstruction of the Pañcatantra, not the textus simplicior. A scholarly reference list says Olivelle's book is a new translation of Edgerton's 1924 text, and Wikipedia's 'List of Panchatantra stories' gives Edgerton's reconstruction as the basis of Olivelle 1997/2006. So the repo key ('Textus simplicior unless noted … Tr.: Olivelle 1997') is internally mismatched. Both verses were verified only in the textus-simplicior-type text (GRETIL vispancu.htm, Jha ed., Kale consulted: Panc_2.136, Panc_3.103). Neither verse occurs in the Tantrākhyāyika e-texts on GRETIL (ttrkhy1u/ttrkhy2u). A reader who follows the REF to Olivelle may not find them. The 2a course wording also says the verse 'also appears' in the Pañcatantra without noting that the Pañcatantra's last line is different (विशन्ति वदने, not प्रविशन्ति मुखे).
corrections.corrected_wording: 2a: "The Hitopadeśa (introduction, verse 36 in common editions) has this verse. The common version of the Pañcatantra (the textus simplicior, Book 2, the weaver Somilaka's story) has it too, with a slightly different last line: न हि सुप्तस्य सिंहस्य विशन्ति वदने मृगाः." Caption: "Hitopadeśa, Prastāvikā 36 (also Pañcatantra, textus simplicior, Book 2)". 3a: "Its second line also appears in the common version (textus simplicior) of the Pañcatantra (Book 3, the tale of the hare and the partridge) …". REFERENCES fix (for Pass C): name a Sanskrit textus-simplicior edition for the panchatantra key, e.g. 'Sanskrit text: ed. M.R. Kale (Motilal Banarsidass) / ed. R. Jha (Chowkhamba 1991)', and add 'Olivelle 1997 translates Edgerton's 1924 reconstruction and may lack textus-simplicior verses', or create a separate key for the textus simplicior.

corrections.item: 3a. New REFERENCES key sternbach1974 / [REF:sternbach1974 3587], and the caption 'source untraced'
corrections.problem: The key's date and the bibliographic evidence (de Jong's review of vol. 1, 1974) do not cover no. 3587. De Jong says vol. 1 covers a–anve and holds 1,873 subhāṣitas. अष्टादश… comes after अन्वे in alphabetical order, so no. 3587 is in a later volume, probably vol. 2 (1976); I did not see the volume itself. Separately, EDITORIAL_GUIDELINES §2 rule 3 ('No locus → no quote') needs a locus in the caption, and the only locus available is the anthology number.

Sternbach (ed.), *Mahā-subhāṣita-saṃgraha*, 8 vols., Hoshiarpur: Vishveshvaranand Vedic Research Institute, 1974– (Vishveshvaranand Indological Series 64 ff.); vol. 1 (1974) = nos. 1–1873. Cited by subhāṣita number." Either rename the key (e.g. sternbach) or note that no. 3587 is in a later volume (probably vol. 2, 1976). Caption: "Traditional verse, Mahā-subhāṣita-saṃgraha no. 3587 (original source untraced). Second line also in Pañcatantra (textus simplicior), Book 3."

EDITORIAL_GUIDELINES §3 says a banned claim may appear 'only as documented errors (e.g. in the improvement report), never as course content'. STYLE_GUIDE §4 rule 5 adds 'may not appear even inside callouts except as *documented errors of 1.x*'. Either (a) keep the 1b HISTORY callout and log the finding in research/verification-log.md without adding it to §3, or (b) add it to §3 with an explicit carve-out, for example: "'ahiṃsā paramo dharmaḥ, dharmahiṃsā tathaiva ca' quoted as one Mahābhārata verse (may appear only in a HISTORY callout that labels the second line unattested in the critical edition)", and amend STYLE_GUIDE §4 rule 5 to match."

corrections.item: 2a. Verdict sentences on the Hitopadeśa–Pañcatantra link, the Sternbach variants and 'idle sons'
corrections.problem: Three small overstatements. (1) Hit 0.9 says the work is drawn 'from the Pañcatantra and another book' (pañcatantrāt tathānyasmād granthād ākṛṣya). That is consistent with the shared verse, but it does not 'explain' it. The textus simplicior is a late recension, so which way the borrowing ran is not established, and the verse also floats in anthologies. Hit 0.33 and 0.36 do sit side by side as Panc 2.135–136, which supports some literary link but not its direction. (2) MSS 6890 is not 'another first line'. It is a variant of the same first line (udyamenaiva kāryāṇi sidhyanti na manorathaiḥ) with the Pañcatantra-type last line. Only 6887 and 6911 have different first lines. (3) In the course wording, 'idle sons' is not what the text says. The sons are anadhigataśāstrāṇām … nityam unmārgagāminām, 'who had not learned the śāstras and were always straying' (prose before Hit 0.12).
corrections.corrected_wording: Verdict: "The Hitopadeśa says it draws on 'the Pañcatantra and another book' (Hit 0.9), which is consistent with the shared verse (Hit 0.33 and 0.36 appear together as Pañc. 2.135–136 in the textus simplicior), though the direction of borrowing is not established. The lion half-line also circulates with other first lines (MSS 6887, 6911) and with a variant of this first line (MSS 6890)." Course: "…King Sudarśana thinks of it while worrying about his unschooled, wayward sons, just before he finds them a teacher."

corrections.item: 3b. Gloss line for अष्टादशपुराणेषु
corrections.problem: The gloss lists अष्टादश and पुराणेषु as if they were two words, but the printed verse (and MSS 3587) has a single compound, अष्टादशपुराणेषु. Item 4 also says saying 3 has no joins between words, so learners could take अष्ट + दश → अष्टादश for vowel sandhi. It is not: अष्टा- is the special form the numeral takes in 18–38 (Whitney §476e, checked).
corrections.corrected_wording: "अष्टादशपुराणेषु (aṣṭādaśapurāṇeṣu) 'in the eighteen Purāṇas': one compound, अष्टादश 'eighteen' + पुराणेषु 'in the Purāṇas'. (अष्टा- is the form अष्ट takes in the numbers 18–38, not a sandhi.) [REF:whitney1889 §476]"

items.verdict: (a) COGNATE. No arrow. Both descend from PIE *méh₂tēr. Latin māter and Greek mḗtēr are further siblings.
items.evidence: Etymonline 'mother' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/mother): OE mōdor < PGmc *mōdēr < PIE *mater-, with Skt mātar- and Lat. māter. The repo already verified this set: research/verification-log.md rows for l04 §13 and v2.c02.l02 (kinship shelf).
items.course_wording: मातृ (mātṛ, nominative माता) and English *mother* are cognates. Both descend from the Proto-Indo-European word for 'mother', and Latin *māter* is a third sibling. English did not borrow the word. Both languages inherited it.

items.verdict: (a) COGNATE for both. Latin pater is a sibling in another language, not an English word. English paternal/patriarch come from Latin and would be type (c). father shows Grimm's Law p > f.
items.evidence: Etymonline 'father' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/father): PIE *pəter- (*ph₂tḗr) > Skt pitar-, Gk/Lat. pater, OE fæder. Etymonline calls it the classic example of Grimm's Law. The repo already confirmed this as the kinship shelf (verification-log, v2.c02 l02).
items.course_wording: पितृ (pitṛ, nominative पिता), Latin *pater* and English *father* are three parallel descendants of one Proto-Indo-European word. English turned the old *p* into *f* by a regular sound change (Grimm's Law). Words like *paternal* reached English later, from Latin.

items.verdict: (a) COGNATE. PIE *bʰréh₂tēr. Latin frāter is a sibling. English fraternal is type (c), from Latin.
items.evidence: Etymonline 'brother' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/brother): OE brōþor < PIE *bhrater-, with Skt bhrā́tar-, Gk phrā́tēr, Lat. frāter. The repo already verified the kinship shelf.
items.course_wording: भ्रातृ (bhrātṛ, nominative भ्राता), Latin *frāter* and English *brother* are cognates inherited from Proto-Indo-European. There is no borrowing in either direction.

items.verdict: new: (a) COGNATE (PIE *néwos). novel: (c), from Latin novellus (diminutive of novus) via Italian novella (the noun, 1560s) and Old French novel (the adjective). Latin novus is the cognate of नव.
items.evidence: Etymonline *newo- and 'new' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/new): Skt navaḥ, Lat. novus, Gk neos. Etymonline 'novel' (https://www.etymonline.com/search?q=novel) and Wiktionary 'novel': Italian novella < Lat. novellus, dim. of novus. The repo already handles the नव 'new' vs नवन् 'nine' homophony (verification-log, v1.c04).
items.course_wording: नव (nava) 'new' and English *new* are cognates. *Novel* is a cousin word: English took it from Latin *novellus* 'new, young', and Latin *novus* is itself a cognate of नव. Note that नव also means 'nine' (stem नवन्). These are two different words, with English cognates *nine* and *new*.

items.verdict: (a) COGNATE. PIE *h₁nómn̥. The Sanskrit stem is नामन् (nāman); नाम is the nominative/accusative. Latin nōmen is a sibling, and English noun/nominal come from it (type c).
items.evidence: Etymonline *no-men- (https://www.etymonline.com/word/*no-men-): Skt nāma, Gk onoma, Lat. nōmen, OE nama. Already verified in the repo (verification-log: नामन् ~ nōmen ~ name, v1 l02 §13).
items.course_wording: नाम (nāma; stem नामन्) and English *name* are cognates, both inherited from Proto-Indo-European. Latin *nōmen* is a sibling, and from it English later took *noun*.

items.verdict: three: (a) COGNATE (PIE *tréyes; Skt nom. pl. trayaḥ). triple: (c), from Latin triplus (tri- + -plus '-fold'). Latin trēs/tri- is the cognate.
items.evidence: Etymonline 'triple' and 'tri-' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/triple, https://www.etymonline.com/word/tri-): Latin triplus; PIE *trei- with Skt trayas. Matches the repo's numeral shelf (verification-log, v1.c05 l01/l02).
items.course_wording: त्रि (tri), Latin *trēs* and English *three* are parallel descendants of the Proto-Indo-European numeral. *Triple* came into English from Latin *triplus*, so it is a cousin through Latin, not a word from Sanskrit.

items.verdict: two: (a) COGNATE (PIE *dwóh₁). dual: (c), from Latin duālis < duo, attested c. 1600 as a grammatical term.
items.evidence: Etymonline 'dual' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/dual): Latin dualis < duo < PIE *dwo-. The root page lists Skt dvau. The repo numeral shelf confirms द्वि ~ duo ~ two.
items.course_wording: द्वि (dvi), Latin *duo* and English *two* are cognates. *Dual* is a cousin through Latin *duālis*. Sanskrit's own grammatical dual is द्विवचन (dvivacana), the 'two-number'.

items.verdict: tooth: (a) COGNATE (PIE *h₁dónts > PGmc *tanþs > OE tōþ; English lost the n). dental: (c), from French dental / Medieval Latin dentālis < Latin dēns, dentis (1590s). The 1.x '(Dent)' is the French/Latin form.
items.evidence: Etymonline *dent- and 'dental' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/*dent-, https://www.etymonline.com/word/dental): Skt danta, Gk odont-, Lat. dēns, Lith. dantis, OE tōð, Goth. tunþus.
items.course_wording: दन्त (danta) and English *tooth* are cognates. The *n* survives in German *Zahn* and Gothic *tunþus* but was lost in English. *Dental* comes from Latin *dēns, dentis*, the Latin cognate. Phoneticians call त थ द ध न 'dental' (Sanskrit दन्त्य) for the same reason.

items.verdict: know: (a) COGNATE (PIE *ǵneh₃-; also English can, ken). gnosis: (c), from Greek gnôsis (in English from 1703). Latin (g)nōscere, the source of cognition and ignore, is another type (c) route.
items.evidence: Etymonline *gno- and 'gnosis' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/*gno-, https://www.etymonline.com/word/gnosis). The repo already verified जानाति ~ know ~ gnōsis (verification-log, v2.c04 l01 §13).
items.course_wording: √ज्ञा (jñā, present जानाति) and English *know* are cognates from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning 'recognize, know'. *Gnosis* is a cousin borrowed from Greek *gnôsis*, the Greek branch of the same family.

items.verdict: (c), and the 1.x quiz answer is FALSE. English video is a 20th-century English formation from Latin videō 'I see' (vidēre). Sanskrit √vid means 'know' (vetti, veda 'I know'), not 'see'. The two share the root PIE *weyd- 'see' (> 'know'). The native English cognates are wit and wise. The 1.x gloss 'vid = to see' is wrong for Sanskrit, and the quiz ''Video' comes from Sanskrit vid ✓' hard-codes a false derivation, the same class of error as the banned October/aṣṭa claim.
items.evidence: Etymonline 'vide' and 'vision' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/vide): Latin videre < PIE *weid- 'to see'. Etymonline 'Veda': Skt veda 'knowledge' < vid- 'to know' < *weid-. 'Wit' < PGmc *wit- < *weid-. The 1.x PDF p.61 quiz (repo Sanskritam-Curriculum.pdf).
items.course_wording: √विद् (vid) 'know' (as in वेद veda 'knowledge') and Latin *vidēre* 'see' are cognates. 'Seeing' and 'knowing' were one idea in their common ancestor. English *video* was built from Latin *videō* 'I see', so it is a cousin, not a loan from Sanskrit. English's own inherited relatives are *wit* and *wise*.

items.verdict: (c), and the 1.x quiz ''Ignite' comes from Agni ✓' is FALSE as a derivation. ignite < Latin ignīre/ignītus < ignis 'fire'. agni ~ ignis (~ Lith. ugnis, OCS ognĭ) are cognates from PIE *h₁n̥gʷnis (reconstructions vary: *h₁n̥gʷnis / *egni-). English fire comes from a different PIE word (*péh₂wr̥).
items.evidence: Wikipedia '*H₁n̥gʷnis' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/*H%E2%82%81n%CC%A5g%CA%B7nis). IE-CoR cognate set 774 (https://iecor.clld.org/cognatesets/774): Lith. ugnìs, Skt agní-, Lat. ignis. Etymonline 'pyre' notes PIE had two fire words. The repo v2.c02.l03 already prints a correct FACT callout.
items.course_wording: अग्नि (agni) and Latin *ignis* 'fire' are cognates, parallel descendants of one Proto-Indo-European word. English *ignite* and *igneous* came later from Latin, so they are cousins through Latin, not borrowings from Sanskrit. English *fire* comes from a different ancient word.

items.verdict: (a) COGNATE. PIE *yugóm (root *yewg- 'join'). Latin iugum and Greek zygón are siblings; English zygote, conjugal and junction are type (c). युग's base sense is 'yoke, pair'; 'age of the world' is a later extended sense.
items.evidence: Etymonline *yeug- (https://www.etymonline.com/word/*yeug-): Skt yugam 'yoke', yunakti/yunjati 'binds', yogaḥ 'union'; Hitt. yugan, Gk zygon, Lat. iugum, OE geoc.
items.course_wording: युग (yuga) 'yoke' and English *yoke* are cognates. Latin *iugum* and Greek *zygón* are further siblings. In Sanskrit the word later also came to mean a world-age (as in कलियुग).

items.item: योग (yoga) / yoga, printed by 1.x under युग
items.verdict: (b) LOAN from Sanskrit, but from योग (yoga, 'yoking, union'), not from युग. योग and युग are separate Sanskrit nouns from the same root √युज्. English yoga is attested from c. 1820. Sources differ on the path: Etymonline routes it 'from Hindi yoga, from Sanskrit', while Wiktionary says borrowed directly from Sanskrit. So do not assert a path. yogi is older (1610s, via Hindi).
items.evidence: Etymonline 'yoga' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/yoga): 1820, 'yogu', from Hindi < Skt yoga 'union, yoking' < PIE *yeug-. Wiktionary 'yoga' (https://en.wiktionary.com/wiki/yoga): 'Borrowed from Sanskrit योग'. The repo l04 already treats yoga as a genuine loan (verification-log).
items.course_wording: English *yoga* is a genuine loanword from Sanskrit योग (yoga) 'yoking, union', borrowed in the early 19th century. योग and युग (yuga) are two different Sanskrit words built on the same root √युज् (yuj) 'to join, harness'. So English has both a borrowed relative (*yoga*) and an inherited one (*yoke*) of this root.

items.verdict: (d) FALSE: unrelated. juggle (late 14th c., jogelen; partly a back-formation from juggler) < Old French jogler < Late Latin ioculāre / Classical Latin ioculārī 'to jest' < ioculus, diminutive of iocus 'jest' (the source of joke and jocular). Wiktionary and Etymonline trace iocus to Proto-Italic *jokos < PIE *yek- 'speak' (the 'word' > 'joke' step is a reconstruction). That is a different root from *yewg- 'join'. The 1.x error probably comes from the surface likeness of Latin iugum 'yoke' and iocus 'joke'. IR-033 in analysis/IMPROVEMENT_REPORT.md already flags it.
items.evidence: Etymonline 'juggle' and 'juggler' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/juggle, https://www.etymonline.com/word/juggler): OF jogler < L. ioculari 'to jest'. Dictionary.com 'juggle' (https://www.dictionary.com/browse/Juggle). Wiktionary 'iocus' (https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/iocus): Proto-Italic *jokos < PIE *yek- 'to speak'. Etymonline 'joke'/'jocular'. I did not reach de Vaan's Latin etymological dictionary, so the PIE step for iocus rests on Wiktionary/Etymonline.
items.course_wording: Only as a documented 1.x error: 'juggle' is NOT related to युग or *yoke*. It comes through Old French from Latin *ioculārī* 'to jest', a relative of English *joke* and *jocular*. A similar sound is not evidence. Relatedness is shown by regular sound correspondences. (Do not print the PIE root of *iocus*. It is not needed and is less certain.)

items.verdict: (a) COGNATE, both words. PIE *médʰyos > OE midd, middel. Latin medius is a sibling; English medium, median and medieval are type (c).
items.evidence: Etymonline *medhyo- family (https://www.etymonline.com/word/medio-, https://www.etymonline.com/word/midst): Skt madhyaḥ, Av. maidiia-, Gk mesos, Lat. medius, Goth. midjis, OE midd.
items.course_wording: मध्य (madhya) 'middle' and English *mid* and *middle* are cognates from Proto-Indo-European. Latin *medius* is a sibling, and English later borrowed *medium* and *median* from it.

items.verdict: (c), both words. voice < Old French voiz < Latin vōx (acc. vōcem). vocal < Latin vōcālis. वाच् ~ vōx are cognates from PIE *wekʷ- 'speak'. English has no everyday native cognate.
items.evidence: Etymonline 'voice', 'vox' and *wekw- (https://www.etymonline.com/word/voice, https://www.etymonline.com/word/*wekw-): Skt vakti 'speaks', vacas- 'word'; Lat. vox, vocare.
items.course_wording: वाच् (vāc) 'speech, voice' and Latin *vōx* 'voice' are cognates. English *voice* and *vocal* came from the Latin branch, through French and Latin, so they are cousins of वाच्, not borrowings from Sanskrit.

items.verdict: night: (a) COGNATE (PIE *nókʷts > PGmc *nahts > OE niht). nocturnal: (c), from Late Latin nocturnālis < nox, noctis. Note: नक्त n. 'night' and नक्तम् adv. 'by night' are mainly Vedic or literary. The everyday classical words are रात्रि and निशा. The 1.x PDF misprints the headword.
items.evidence: Etymonline 'night' and 'noct-' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/night, https://www.etymonline.com/word/noct-): Gk nyx, Lat. nox, Skt naktam 'at night', Lith. naktis.
items.course_wording: नक्त (nakta) 'night' (more often seen as नक्तम् naktam 'by night') and English *night* are cognates. *Nocturnal* reached English from Latin *nox, noctis*, the Latin cognate.

items.verdict: stand: (a) COGNATE (PIE *steh₂-; Germanic *standaną adds a nasal). state (via Old French estat < Latin status) and station (via Old French < Latin statiō): (c). Sanskrit present तिष्ठति (tiṣṭhati) has reduplication like Greek hístēmi and Latin sistō.
items.evidence: Etymonline *sta- / 'status' / 'stance' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/status): Skt tisthati, Av. histaiti, Gk histēmi, Lat. stare, status, statio, OE standan.
items.course_wording: √स्था (sthā, present तिष्ठति) 'stand' and English *stand* are cognates. *State* and *station* came into English from Latin *status* and *statiō*, which belong to the Latin branch of the same family. They are cousins, not borrowings from Sanskrit.

items.verdict: foot: (a) COGNATE (PIE *pṓds; Grimm's Law p > f, d > t). pedal (Latin pedālis) and pedestrian (Latin pedester): (c), from Latin pēs, pedis. CAUTION: the closest Sanskrit match for 'foot' is the root noun पद् (pad, Vedic nom. pā́t) or पाद (pāda). पद (pada) is mainly 'step, footprint, position; word', from the same root.
items.evidence: Wiktionary 'pes' (https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/pes): Lat. pēs < Proto-Italic *pets < PIE *pṓds, compare Skt पद् (pád), Gk poús, OE fōt. IE-CoR cognate set 225 (https://iecor.clld.org/cognatesets/225): Vedic pā́t. Etymonline *ped- (https://www.etymonline.com/word/*ped-).
items.course_wording: Sanskrit पाद (pāda) / पद् (pad) 'foot', Latin *pēs, pedis* and English *foot* are cognates. *Foot* shows Grimm's Law (p→f, d→t). *Pedal* and *pedestrian* came later from Latin, so they are cousins. (पद pada 'step; word' belongs to the same root.)

items.verdict: (a) COGNATE. PIE *h₁widʰéwh₂; Latin vidua, OE widuwe, OCS vĭdova, Old Irish fedb. A traditional Indian analysis reads it as vi- 'without' + dhava 'husband', i.e. 'husbandless'. MW gives this only 'according to some'. Because the word is inherited from PIE, historians treat that split as a later reinterpretation. A secondary source (wisdomlib, apparently quoting Macdonell & Keith's Vedic Index) says dhava 'man' is not found before the Nirukta and owes its existence to a misreading of vidhavā. I could not verify that attribution directly.
items.evidence: Wiktionary विधवा and 'vidua' (https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%A7%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%BE, https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/vidua): PIE *h₁widʰéwh₂. Etymonline 'widow' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/widow): root 'separate'. MW adhavā entry (via wisdomlib https://www.wisdomlib.org/definition/vidhava): 'usually vi-dhavā'; 'according to some fr. vi + dhava'. The dhava back-formation remark is from wisdomlib 'Dhava' (https://www.wisdomlib.org/definition/dhava).
items.course_wording: FACT: विधवा (vidhavā) and English *widow* (Latin *vidua*) are cognates inherited from Proto-Indo-European. TRADITION: Traditional Sanskrit word analysis explains विधवा as वि + धव, 'without a husband'. Historical linguistics treats this as a later reading of a much older inherited word. (Do not print the 'dhava is a back-formation' claim unless Macdonell & Keith 1912 s.v. dhava is checked.)

items.verdict: (c), and the 1.x quiz ''Serpent' comes from Sarpa ✓' is FALSE as a derivation. serpent < Old French < Latin serpēns, present participle of serpere 'creep'. सर्प < √सृप् 'creep' (sarpati). Both come from PIE *serp-. Greek herpein (source of herpes and herpetology) is a further sibling. English snake is from a different root.
items.evidence: Etymonline 'serpent' (https://www.etymonline.com/word/serpent): Lat. serpentem < serpere < PIE *serp- 'crawl, creep'; Skt sarpati, sarpaḥ; Gk herpein. UT Austin Indo-European Lexicon (https://lrc.la.utexas.edu/lex/master/1705): Skt sárpati. Etymonline 'snake': separate root *sneg-.
items.course_wording: सर्प (sarpa) 'snake, the creeper' (from √सृप् 'creep') and Latin *serpēns* 'creeping thing' are cognates. English *serpent* came from the Latin branch through French, so it is a cousin of सर्प, not a borrowing from it. English *snake* is unrelated to both.

items.verdict: MODERN COINAGE from classical parts: a calque (loan-translation) of tele-vision, with दूर 'far' = tele-, and दर्शन 'seeing, sight' = vision. Classical Sanskrit has the adjective dūradarśin 'far-seeing, prudent' (Amarakośa, Rāmāyaṇa per Böhtlingk-Roth). A classical noun dūradarśana is NOT confirmed. I found no source on who coined the Hindi/Sanskrit term or when. As a broadcaster name, Doordarshan began experimentally in Delhi on 15 Sep 1959 and was separated from All India Radio on 1 Apr 1976.
items.evidence: Wikipedia 'Doordarshan' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doordarshan): 'distant vision', 15 Sep 1959. PIB 2023 document (https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2023/sep/doc2023915251801.pdf) and Prasar Bharati 'About Doordarshan' (https://prasarbharati.gov.in/?p=2241): separation 1 Apr 1976. Dūradarśin senses from wisdomlib/kosha mirrors of MW, Apte and Böhtlingk-Roth (https://de.wisdomlib.org/definition/duradarshin).
items.course_wording: दूरदर्शन (dūradarśana) 'television' is a modern word built from two classical parts: दूर (dūra) 'far' + दर्शन (darśana) 'seeing'. It translates the Greek-Latin *tele-vision* piece by piece (a 'calque'). India's public broadcaster took the name Doordarshan; its first experimental broadcast was in Delhi in 1959. (Do not name a coiner.)
