items.verdict: CLASSICAL WORD WITH A NEW MEANING. The classical sense is 'a voice from the sky / heaven', the disembodied voice of epic and purāṇic narrative (compare aśarīrī vāṇī, 'bodiless voice'). It was applied to radio in the 1930s. Who coined it is disputed in the sources: (1) usually credited to M.V. Gopalaswamy, who named his private Mysore station (1935/1936) 'Akashvani'; (2) Wikipedia says the Telugu/Kannada scholar Rallapalli Ananta Krishna Sharma suggested the name to him; (3) Britannica says the poet Narendra Sharma reportedly suggested it for official use; (4) Tagore wrote a poem 'Akashvani' for the Calcutta shortwave inauguration (1938 per Britannica, 1939 per RadioInfo Asia). AIR's official on-air name since 1956. Sources giving 1957 likely confuse it with Vividh Bharati (3 Oct 1957). In May 2023 Prasar Bharati made 'Akashvani' the only on-air name. The 1.x quiz 'literally means sky-voice' is acceptable as FACT about the parts.
items.evidence: Wikipedia 'All India Radio' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_India_Radio). Britannica 'All India Radio (AIR)' (https://www.britannica.com/topic/All-India-Radio). The News Minute 'AIR at 80' (https://www.thenewsminute.com/features/air-80-how-it-was-mysuru-brought-radio-alive-india-44734). RadioInfo Asia (https://radioinfo.asia/news/all-india-radio-goes-off-air-replaced-by-akashvani/). Classical sense via kosha (https://kosha.sanskrit.today/word/sa/आकाशवाणी): 'voice from heaven', and MW aśarīra 'not coming from a visible body (as a voice)', Rāmāyaṇa and Kathāsaritsāgara.
items.course_wording: FACT: आकाशवाणी (ākāśavāṇī) = आकाश (ākāśa) 'sky' + वाणी (vāṇī) 'voice'. In classical Sanskrit literature it means a voice from the sky, a divine voice heard without a speaker. HISTORY: In the 1930s the old word was given a new job. It is usually credited to M.V. Gopalaswamy's private radio station in Mysore (1935–36), though sources credit different people with suggesting it. All India Radio adopted Ākāśavāṇī as its official on-air name in 1956.
items.register: FACT (structure, classical sense); HISTORY (application to radio, hedged); TRADITION if an epic 'voice from the sky' scene is quoted (needs text + locus)

For the naming history: no key, needs new REFERENCES entry: 'All India Radio (AIR)', *Encyclopaedia Britannica* (online), https://www.britannica.com/topic/All-India-Radio (accessed 2026-10). items.verdict: MODERN COINAGE: a calque of inter-net, with अन्तर् 'between, within' = inter-, and जाल 'net' = net. Late 20th century; I found no source for coiner or date. It is used in Hindi (अंतर्जाल/अंतरजाल; कम्प्यूटर-free alternatives) and Marathi (आंतरजाल, महाजाल). Do not confuse it with the classical अन्तर्जल (antarjala) 'water within, underwater', which is built on jala 'water'.
items.evidence: HinKhoj 'internet' (https://hinkhojdictionary.com/english-hindi/internet-meaning-in-hindi): अन्तर्जाल/अंतरजाल. Marathi dictionary (आंतरजाल, महाजाल). Classical अन्तर्जल 'underwater' via wisdomlib/Cologne (https://de.wisdomlib.org/definition/antarjala).
items.course_wording: अन्तर्जाल (antarjāla) 'internet' is a modern coinage that translates English *inter-net* part by part: अन्तर् (antar) 'between' + जाल (jāla) 'net'. The parts are classical. The compound is new.
items.ref: [REF:monierwilliams1899 s.vv. अन्तर्, जाल] for the parts. No citable source for the coinage (do not date it).

items.verdict: MODERN COINAGE from classical parts: सम् (sam) 'together, completely' + गणक (gaṇaka), classically 'arithmetician, reckoner, astrologer' (Apte). I found no source for coiner or date (20th century). It is the standard term in Marathi (government glossary). In Hindi it exists but कंप्यूटर is far more common. The 1.x gloss 'counter' is acceptable for गणक if hedged.
items.evidence: Apte scan via Cologne (https://sanskrit-lexicon.uni-koeln.de/scans/AP90Scan/AP90Scanpdf/pg_0448.pdf): gaṇaka 'arithmetician, astrologer'. Maharashtra govt. Marathi dictionary (https://shabdakosh.marathi.gov.in/node?page=1791): संगणक. Shabdkosh Hindi (https://www.shabdkosh.com/hi/dictionary/english-hindi/computer/computer-meaning-in-hindi). ProZ discussion: कम्प्यूटर more common in Hindi.
items.course_wording: संगणक (saṃgaṇaka) 'computer' is a modern word built from old parts: सम् (sam) 'together' + गणक (gaṇaka), which in classical Sanskrit meant a reckoner, an arithmetician or astrologer who calculates. Marathi uses संगणक every day. Everyday Hindi mostly says कंप्यूटर.

items.verdict: MODERN COINAGE, and the exact form is NOT attested in any source I could find. Attested modern Sanskrit renderings: चलदूरवाणी (caladūravāṇī; Radhakant Thakur's 2010 Sanskrit poem on the mobile phone, Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeetha, Tirupati) and जङ्गमदूरवाणी (jaṅgamadūravāṇī; Kosha). Hindi uses दूरभाष 'telephone' officially, with सचल दूरभाष or simply मोबाइल for mobile phone. There is no single standard. The 1.x breakdown चल 'moving' + दूर 'far' + भाष 'speech' is structurally fine.
items.evidence: Kosha 'digital cellular phone' (https://kosha.sanskrit.today/word/en/digital%20cellular%20phone): जङ्गमदूरवाणी. Exotic India listing for Thakur's 2010 poem (https://exoticindiaart.com/book/details/mobile-phone-poem-in-sanskrit-nai606): चलदूरवाणी. HinKhoj दूरभाष = telephone (https://hinkhojdictionary.com/hindi-english/दूरभाष-meaning-in-english).
items.course_wording: Modern Sanskrit has several competing words for 'mobile phone', all built the same way: 'moving' + 'far' + 'speech/voice'. Examples are चलदूरवाणी (caladūravāṇī) and जङ्गमदूरवाणी (jaṅgamadūravāṇī). The pattern starts from दूरभाष (dūrabhāṣa) 'telephone' (far-speech), the standard word on Hindi letterheads. (Either drop चलदूरभाष or present it as 'one possible coinage', not as THE word.)

items.verdict: CLASSICAL WORD WITH A NEW MEANING. The 1.x etymology is FALSE. vimāna = vi- + √mā 'to measure (out), traverse'. In the Vedic texts it means 'measuring out, traversing; a measure'. मान (māna) never means 'vehicle'. (1) māna from √man = opinion, notion, self-regard, pride, honour (MW). (2) māna from √mā = measuring, a measure, a standard (Apte). The prefix vi- means 'apart, asunder, out, dis-', not 'special'. Classical senses of vimāna (MW, as reproduced on Wikipedia; confirm exact wording): a car or chariot of the gods, a mythical self-moving aerial car, sometimes like a palace (e.g. Rāvaṇa's Puṣpaka in the Rāmāyaṇa); the palace of an emperor (especially seven-storied); a temple or shrine of a particular form (the South Indian temple tower is still called the vimāna); any car or vehicle; a ship. 'Airplane' in modern Hindi and Sanskrit is a 20th-century extension of the 'aerial car' sense. Related caution: the 'Vaimānika Śāstra' is a 20th-century text. Mukunda et al. (IISc, 1974) found it cannot be dated before 1904 and that its craft could not fly.
items.evidence: Wikipedia 'Vimana' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vimana), reproducing MW 'car or chariot of the gods… self-moving aerial car… palace… seven stories'. A scholarly description (via encyclopedia.pub) gives Vedic vi-MĀ 'measure, mete out, pass over, traverse'. MW māna (√man) 'opinion, conception… pride… honour' (https://sanskrit-lexicon.uni-koeln.de/scans/MW72Scan/MW72Scanpdf/pg_0770.pdf). Apte māna n. 'measuring; a measure, standard' (quoted at https://list.indology.info/pipermail/indology/2021-January/053947.html). Mukunda et al. 1974 PDF (https://cgpl.iisc.ac.in/oldwebcontent/site/Portals/0/Publications/ReferedJournal/ACriticalStudyOfTheWorkVaimanikaShastra.pdf).
items.course_wording: FACT: विमान (vimāna) comes from वि (vi) + √मा (mā) 'to measure out, traverse'. In the oldest texts it means 'measuring out' or 'traversing'. (मान māna means 'measure' or 'honour, pride', never 'vehicle'.) In classical literature a विमान is a chariot of the gods, a palace or a temple tower. Modern Hindi and Sanskrit gave the old word a new job: 'aeroplane'. TRADITION: In the Rāmāyaṇa, Rāvaṇa's Puṣpaka vimāna is a flying palace-chariot (cite kāṇḍa.sarga.verse before printing).
items.register: FACT (etymology, senses); TRADITION (epic flying cars, with locus); HISTORY only if the Vaimānika Śāstra is mentioned
items.ref: [REF:monierwilliams1899 s.v. विमान]; [REF:apte1890 s.v. मान]. If the Vaimānika note is used: no key, needs new REFERENCES entry: H.S. Mukunda, S.M. Deshpande, H.R. Nagendra, A. Prabhu & S.P. Govindaraju, 'A Critical Study of the Work "Vyamanika Shastra"', *Scientific Opinion* (1974), pp. 5–12.

items.item: 1.x quiz: 'The genius of Sanskrit: you can create new words by combining roots + prefixes + suffixes'
items.verdict: OVERCLAIM. Building words from roots, prefixes and suffixes, plus compounding, is ordinary across languages. English does it (un-break-able, re-write-r; tele-vision is itself Greek tele- + Latin vision), as do German (Fern-seh-er), Turkish and Arabic (root-and-pattern). 'Genius' is marketing language that STYLE_GUIDE §7 bans. The quiz's distractors ('Random invention', 'Copying other languages') are filler, violating STYLE_GUIDE §5. What IS defensible: (1) Sanskrit's derivational system is large and highly productive, and it is the machinery behind every coinage in this unit; (2) the Pāṇinian grammar describes it explicitly. Prefixes (upasarga) are defined at Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.58–59. Root-suffixes (kṛt) are defined at 3.1.93 kṛd atiṅ. Nominal-stem suffixes (taddhita) fall under the heading rule 4.1.76 taddhitāḥ, which runs to the end of book 5. Whitney §1139 discusses the primary (kṛt) vs secondary (taddhita) split.
items.evidence: Sūtra loci via Wikipedia 'Upasarga' (1.4.58–59), learnsanskrit.org kṛt intro (3.1.93) (https://www.learnsanskrit.org/vyakarana/krt/introduction/) and taddhita intro (4.1.76) (https://learnsanskrit.org/vyakarana/taddhita/introduction/), and arXiv 1512.05670 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.05670), all secondary. Whitney §1139 on the primary/secondary split via Wikisource search snippet (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Sanskrit_Grammar_by_Whitney_p1.djvu/447). Typology: Haspelmath & Sims, Understanding Morphology, ch. 3 'Affixation and compounding' (TOC only). For cross-language prevalence use English examples, which are self-evident, rather than a scale claim.
items.course_wording: FACT: Sanskrit builds words systematically: a root (धातु), plus prefixes (उपसर्ग), plus suffixes (कृत् after roots, तद्धित after nouns), plus compounding. संगणक, दूरदर्शन and अन्तर्जाल were all made this way. Many languages work like this, English included (*un-break-able*; *tele-vision* itself). What is unusual about Sanskrit is how completely its grammarians catalogued the machinery: Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī defines the prefixes (1.4.59) and the two suffix families (3.1.93, 4.1.76). Suggested quiz replacement: 'How were modern words like संगणक and अन्तर्जाल formed?' Key: (a) classical roots + prefixes + suffixes / compounding. Distractors from real confusions: (b) borrowed whole from English; (c) found ready-made in classical texts (true only of आकाशवाणी/विमान-type words); (d) translated sound-for-sound from English.
items.register: FACT (the Pāṇini clause becomes TRADITION if phrased 'According to Pāṇini…')

corrections.item: विधवा (vidhavā) / widow: TRADITION half of course_wording
corrections.problem: Under-sourced, and the attribution is probably wrong. STYLE_GUIDE §4 rule 3 says a TRADITION block must name its source text or tradition, but the wording only says 'Traditional Sanskrit word analysis'. The oldest traditional etymology, Yāska's Nirukta (usually cited as 3.15), does not give vi + dhava 'husband'. A JRAS article 'On the Interpretation of the Veda' (cambridge.org) summarises the passage this way: vidhavā = vidhātṛkā 'without a supporter', or, according to Carmaśiras (a predecessor of Yāska), from vidhavana / vidhāvana. The vi + dhava reading, analysed as vigato dhavo yasyāḥ sā, belongs to later commentators and lexicographers. Two further problems with the verdict. (1) I could not confirm MW's wording 'according to some fr. vi + dhava'. The only MW text I could confirm (through a Buddhist Door mirror) is a-dhavā 'one who has no husband, a widow (usually vi-dhavā, q.v.)'. (2) REFERENCES.md has no Nirukta key, so the Nirukta point needs a new entry. Macdonell & Keith's Vedic Index (2 vols, London: John Murray, 1912) is confirmed as a real work, but its dhava entry is still unchecked.
corrections.corrected_wording: FACT: विधवा (vidhavā) and English *widow* (Latin *vidua*) are cognates inherited from Proto-Indo-European. TRADITION: Later Sanskrit commentators read विधवा as 'she whose husband (धव) is gone'. Yāska's Nirukta, the oldest Sanskrit work on etymology, explains it differently, as 'without a supporter' (विधातृका), and also records other explanations. Historical linguistics treats all of these as later readings of a much older inherited word. [Before printing: check the Nirukta locus against the text (usually cited as 3.15) and add a REFERENCES key; name the commentator or kośa for the वि + धव reading; do not quote MW's 'according to some' until it is checked.]

corrections.item: विद् (vid) / video: course_wording sentence "'Seeing' and 'knowing' were one idea in their common ancestor"
corrections.problem: Overclaim and too vague. The standard reconstruction is that PIE *weyd- meant 'see'. Its perfect, 'I have seen', came to mean 'I know'. That is why Sanskrit वेद (veda) 'I know', Greek oîda and Old English wāt/witan (English wit, wot) are all old perfects meaning 'know'. The course should state this concrete mechanism, not say the two were 'one idea'.
corrections.corrected_wording: √विद् (vid) 'know' (as in वेद veda 'knowledge') and Latin *vidēre* 'see' are cognates. In their common ancestor the root meant 'see', and its perfect, 'I have seen', came to mean 'I know'. Sanskrit वेद (veda) 'I know' and Greek *oîda* 'I know' both keep that old perfect. English *video* was built from Latin *videō* 'I see', so it is a cousin, not a loan from Sanskrit. English's own inherited relatives are *wit* and *wise*.

corrections.item: चलदूरभाष (caladūrabhāṣa) = mobile phone: course_wording
corrections.problem: The wording contradicts itself and makes an unsourced historical claim. Both attested examples it gives (चलदूरवाणी, जङ्गमदूरवाणी) are built on दूरवाणी (dūravāṇī), not on दूरभाष, so 'The pattern starts from दूरभाष' does not hold and implies a derivation history that nobody has sourced. दूरभाष is the Hindi official word; modern Sanskrit usually says दूरवाणी. The verdict's 'NOT attested in any source I could find' reports only the researcher's own search. I could not re-check Hindi official usage (चलभाष / चल दूरभाष) because the search budget ran out, so 'drop चलदूरभाष' is not a safe instruction. Presenting it as one possible coinage is safe. If the दूरवाणी forms are printed, the ref also needs MW s.v. वाणी.
corrections.corrected_wording: Modern Sanskrit and Hindi have several competing words for 'mobile phone', all built from the same kind of parts: 'moving' + 'far' + 'speech/voice'. Examples are चलदूरवाणी (caladūravāṇī) and जङ्गमदूरवाणी (jaṅgamadūravāṇī). They extend the telephone words दूरवाणी (dūravāṇī, common in modern Sanskrit) and दूरभाष (dūrabhāṣa, the official Hindi word), both meaning 'far-speech'. चलदूरभाष is one more possible coinage of this type, not THE word.

corrections.item: विमान (vimāna): verdict 'The prefix vi- means apart, asunder, out, dis-, not special'
corrections.problem: Overclaim. MW's entry for the prefix vi- lists 'distinction' and sometimes an intensive sense among its values. Traditional glosses often render vi- as viśeṣa/viśiṣṭa ('special, distinguished'). The real 1.x errors are मान = 'vehicle' and missing the root √मा. 'Special' for vi- is a defensible traditional gloss, not a falsehood. The course_wording is fine because it does not repeat the vi- claim, so only the verdict needs fixing. Mukunda et al. 1974 checks out: its abstract says the text cannot be dated earlier than 1904 and that the heavier-than-air craft are unfeasible.
corrections.corrected_wording: The 1.x etymology is FALSE because मान (māna) never means 'vehicle' and the word is vi- + √mā 'measure out, traverse'. The gloss 'special' for vi- is loose but has traditional precedent (vi- = viśeṣa). The prefix's basic senses are 'apart, asunder, distinction'.

corrections.item: आकाशवाणी (ākāśavāṇī): course_wording FACT sentence and the 1956 sentence
corrections.problem: Under-hedged on two points. (1) 'In classical Sanskrit literature it means a voice from the sky' is printed as FACT. The researcher's own ref note says the compound's listing in MW/Apte is still unconfirmed, and the epic motif is often worded as a 'bodiless voice' (aśarīrī/aśarīriṇī vāk) rather than with this compound. (2) 'adopted Ākāśavāṇī as its official on-air name in 1956': most sources say it was 'officially renamed' or adopted the name in 1956 (one archive, Trinity College Cambridge, gives 1957). 'All India Radio' stayed in use on English broadcasts until the May 2023 order, so 'on-air name' overstates 1956.
corrections.corrected_wording: FACT: आकाशवाणी (ākāśavāṇī) = आकाश (ākāśa) 'sky' + वाणी (vāṇī) 'voice'. In Sanskrit storytelling, a voice from the sky, heard with no speaker in sight, is a familiar device [print only after MW/Apte s.v. आकाश confirms the compound; otherwise say 'the idea of a voice from the sky']. HISTORY: In the 1930s the old word was given a new job. It is usually credited to M.V. Gopalaswamy's private radio station in Mysore (1935–36), though sources credit different people with suggesting it. All India Radio adopted Ākāśavāṇī as its official name in 1956 (most sources), and since 2023 it has been the only name used on air.

corrections.problem: Overclaim. संगणक is the standard word in written, official and school Marathi (the government glossary), but spoken Marathi often uses कॉम्प्युटर. I could not re-verify this with search (budget exhausted), so hedge rather than assert everyday use.
corrections.corrected_wording: संगणक is the standard word in written and official Marathi, while everyday Hindi mostly says कंप्यूटर.

corrections.item: नव (nava) / novel: course_wording 'English took it from Latin novellus'
corrections.problem: Imprecise path. The verdict itself says novel came via Italian novella (the noun, 1560s) and Old French novel (the adjective), not directly from Latin. Other items in the table name the French or Italian step, so this one should too.
corrections.corrected_wording: *Novel* is a cousin word: it reached English through Italian *novella* and Old French *novel*, from Latin *novellus* 'new, young', a diminutive of *novus*. Latin *novus* is itself a cognate of नव.

corrections.item: 'Genius of Sanskrit' quiz: suggested replacement distractors
corrections.problem: Distractor (d) 'translated sound-for-sound from English' nearly duplicates (b) 'borrowed whole from English'. It also sits too close to the calque idea that this same unit teaches: अन्तर्जाल and दूरदर्शन ARE part-by-part translations of English or Greek-Latin words. A student who learned 'calque' could reasonably hesitate between (a) and (d), which goes against STYLE_GUIDE §5's 'plausible errors, not filler' in the opposite direction. The key should acknowledge calquing.
corrections.corrected_wording: Q: How were modern words like संगणक and अन्तर्जाल formed? Key: (a) by combining classical roots, prefixes, suffixes and compounds, often translating the English word part by part. Distractors: (b) borrowed whole from English (like कंप्यूटर); (c) found ready-made with this meaning in classical texts (true only of आकाशवाणी/विमान-type words); (d) made up as new sound-sequences with no older parts.

corrections.item: योग (yoga) / yoga: course_wording 'borrowed in the early 19th century'
corrections.problem: Mildly under-hedged. The c. 1820 date (Etymonline/OED) is a first attestation, not the date of borrowing. *Yogi* is already recorded in the 1610s, and Charles Wilkins's 1785 Bhagavad Gītā translation is reported to use the form 'Yog' (my recollection; not checked, search budget exhausted).
corrections.corrected_wording: English *yoga* is a genuine loanword from Sanskrit योग (yoga) 'yoking, union', first recorded in English in the early 19th century (*yogi* is older).

corrections.item: ज्ञा (jñā) / know, gnosis: verdict 'Latin (g)nōscere, the source of cognition and ignore'
corrections.problem: Imprecise, though not in the course wording. *Ignore* comes from Latin ignōrāre, from ignārus (in- + gnārus), which belongs to the same root but is not derived from (g)nōscere. *Cognition* does come from cognōscere.
corrections.corrected_wording: Latin (g)nōscere (source of *cognition*), and its relative gnārus (behind ignōrāre, the source of *ignore*), are further type (c) routes.
